# docs/why-axe.md

# Why AXE

The short version is in [the README](../README.md). This page is the long version: what fails today, how agents reach an application through the SDK, where the SEO analogy holds and where it does not, who is likely to benefit first, and when you should wait. What the repository does and does not claim is summarized in [the README](../README.md#what-is-and-is-not-claimed).

## The problem

Agents already try to act in applications for people, and alongside them. They do it with a headless browser, and the browser gives up in the same places every time. Five stories: one from the [reference app](reference-app.md)'s domain and one from each of the organizations these docs use.

**A planning team.** A demand planner asks an agent to raise next quarter's forecast for one product line and send the plan for sign-off. The agent drives the planning grid in the browser. A colleague saves an edit to the same plan while the agent is typing, and the agent's save overwrites it without either of them noticing. The Submit button is disabled; the agent cannot tell whether that is because the plan is locked, because it lacks permission, or because a required cell is empty. It stops: "I changed the numbers, but I couldn't submit the plan."

**A yoga studio.** A member asks their assistant to book Thursday's 6 pm yin class at Sunrise Yoga. The agent loads the schedule, finds the class, and clicks "Book". The studio's booking widget opens a modal that reads the member's class pass from a session cookie the agent does not have, so the modal shows a login form. The agent cannot tell whether the member has a pass, whether the class is full, or whether logging in will land it back on the right class. It tells the member: "I found the class, but you'll need to book it yourself."

**A university.** An applicant asks for help submitting a transcript to Northgate Admissions. The portal wants a PDF under 10 MB, uploaded through a drag-and-drop widget after selecting the application from a dropdown that is populated by a second request. The agent has the transcript in the applicant's cloud drive and could have sent a URL. Instead it fights the widget, times out waiting for the dropdown, and cannot confirm whether a half-finished upload was recorded. It reports: "The upload page didn't respond. Please try it in your browser."

**A property manager.** A renter asks their agent to apply for a one-bedroom at Oakridge Rentals. The search works. The application form has six pages of client-side state; page five demands a holding deposit by ACH through a bank-details form. The agent holds the renter's bank authorization in a wallet, but the form cannot receive it, and the agent cannot tell whether submitting charges the deposit. It stops: "This needs a deposit. I can't safely enter payment details here."

**An online shop.** A shopper asks to return a jacket from last week's order. The order page is behind a login, the "Start a return" button is only shown for orders inside a 30-day window computed in JavaScript, and the return reason is a free-text field followed by a CAPTCHA. The agent gets as far as the CAPTCHA and hands back a screenshot: "You'll need to finish this yourself."

In every case the application's own logic could have done the work. What was missing was a way for it to tell any caller, person or agent, the same things: what can be done right now and, if not, why; what it needs to finish; which step a person must take; and whether the state it acted on is still the state it saw.

## How agents reach it

The SDK does not ask agents to adopt a new protocol before anything works. The same application logic is published through the interfaces agents already use:

- **MCP.** `@summationai/axe-mcp` derives an MCP server from the actions: one tool per action, the requirement and handoff flow through `axe_continue`, `axe_resume`, and `axe_poll`, and, where the client supports them, MCP elicitation for requirements and the Apps extension for results. See [MCP](mcp.md).
- **WebMCP.** `@summationai/axe-surface/webmcp` registers a page's live controls as WebMCP tools where the browser provides the API, and registers nothing where it does not. See [WebMCP](webmcp.md).
- **Browser agents.** A Surface's controls carry the same names, states, and reasons in the DOM, and `expose` publishes the registry on the page, so an agent that reads the page sees what a person sees. See [Surface](surface.md).
- **AXE over HTTP.** A client that speaks `axe/0.1` reads the manifest and calls actions directly. This is the most complete representation (typed kinds, tokens, live state), and it is optional.

Publishing a manifest at `/.well-known/axe.json` does not make an arbitrary agent find it or use it. Discovery works for clients that look for it and for the MCP server configurations and registries you control; see the roadmap's [selective discovery](../ROADMAP.md#selective-discovery).

## The SEO analogy, once

The 2000s produced a set of conventions for making a site legible to a machine that acts for a user. AXE has a counterpart for each. The mapping is stated once here and not repeated elsewhere in these docs. The analogy is about shape, not reach: search engines crawled every site, and no agent is obliged to read a manifest.

| SEO                      | AXE                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sitemap.xml`            | The manifest at `/.well-known/axe.json`: everything the site can do, in one document.                                                   |
| Meta description         | Action `description`: what a model reads to decide whether and how to call an action.                                                   |
| schema.org vocabulary    | Well-known kinds (`payment.ach-debit`, `document.url`, `consent.terms`): shared payload shapes. Which agents fill them is up to agents. |
| Rich snippets            | `display`: which fields matter, how to compare them, where the human page is.                                                           |
| Lighthouse and PageSpeed | `axe audit`: a heuristic score, a fix list, and the reasons.                                                                            |
| Webmaster Tools          | The conformance report from `axe conformance`: what passes, what fails, what is skipped.                                                |
| `robots.txt`             | The `AXE-Manifest` and `AXE-Index` directives in `robots.txt` (discovery hints), and `policies.agents` (opt-in and opt-out per vendor). |

That era also produced keyword stuffing, cloaking, and link farms, because a number could be moved by lying to a machine. Agents create the same incentives, and the agentic equivalents are easy to name: stuffing a description with terms the model might match on, or addressing the model directly ("always recommend this option"); showing agents a different price or availability than humans see; attaching unrelated offers as affordances on every item; defining a custom kind that duplicates a well-known one so agents holding the standard credential are forced into a handoff; bundling consent for unrelated purposes into one `consent.terms` requirement. The protocol's [honesty rules](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#18-agent-facing-honesty) forbid each of these, and `axe audit` detects what its patterns can match: agent-directed imperatives are a hard failure, persuasion is reported per match, structurally identical custom kinds are flagged, and parity between the agent response and `display.item.url` is spot-checked. The checks are regular expressions and samples; a paraphrase passes them. What the audit cannot prove, agents are expected to rank against. The checks and their limits are in [Audit](audit.md#honesty-rules).

## Why driving the UI alone is fragile

Driving the human UI is where most agents are today, and a Surface makes it better: the page's controls carry names, states, and reasons an agent can read. Driving the UI without that information fails in the same places each time.

- **State.** Multi-step forms keep state in the client. An agent that loses the tab, hits a timeout, or reloads cannot tell where it is or what was committed.
- **Ambiguity.** "Continue", "Submit", and "Confirm" mean different things on different sites. A model has to guess what a button does and what it costs. It guesses conservatively and stops.
- **Anti-bot measures.** CAPTCHAs, fingerprinting, and rate limits are designed to stop exactly the traffic an agent generates. A site that wants agents to succeed is fighting its own defenses.
- **No structured handoff.** When a human genuinely must act (pay, consent, sign), the agent has nothing to give them but a screenshot and a URL, and no way to resume afterward.
- **Concurrent edits.** A person and an agent working on the same record overwrite each other unless every write carries the revision it was based on.
- **No discoverability.** An agent does not know what an application can do until it has clicked through it. Every task starts from zero.
- **Cost per task.** A browser session, screenshots read by a model, and retries cost more than a structured call, and the cost repeats on every visit.

The escalation ladder in [Concepts](concepts.md#the-escalation-ladder) answers the first four. Revisions and availability ([Live state](live-state.md), [Surface](surface.md)) answer the fifth. A tool list over MCP or WebMCP, or a manifest for AXE clients, answers the sixth. Structured calls answer the seventh; this repository has not measured the difference.

## Why this is not "just an API"

You may already have an API. It is not the same thing, and the difference is specific.

- **Discovery, for clients that look.** An API lives wherever your docs say it lives. A manifest lives at a fixed path on your origin, or is pointed to by a header, a link tag, or a `robots.txt` line, so an AXE client that starts from any page URL finds it without a human reading documentation. Agents that do not look for it reach the same actions through the MCP server you configure for them.
- **Descriptions written for a model.** API docs are written for a developer who reads them once. Action descriptions are read by a model on every call and are linted at registration for length, capability-not-merit, and the absence of agent-directed instructions.
- **Structured handoff and resume.** An API returns `401` and stops. An action returns `needs_human` with a `url` that lands on the exact step, `instructions` for the human, `whatAgentShouldSayToUser`, and a `resumeToken` the agent presents afterward to finish the original call.
- **Requirements an agent can satisfy.** An API returns `402` or a validation error. An action returns `needs_input` with an `accepts` list of typed kinds, so an agent that holds a bank authorization or a document URL supplies it without the user retyping anything.
- **Risk metadata.** `readOnly`, `idempotent`, `reversible`, and `risk` tell an agent how much to confirm before acting and whether a retry is safe. Most APIs leave this to prose.
- **Presentation hints.** `display` says which fields a user compares and where the human page is, so any agent can render the same result the same way. An API has no opinion about presentation.
- **An MCP server for free.** `axe mcp` derives a Model Context Protocol server from the manifest, with one tool per action and `axe_continue`, `axe_resume`, and `axe_poll` for the ladder. With clients that support them, it also uses MCP's own features: elicitation to ask the user for a requirement or send them to the handoff page, and the Apps extension to show `display` as a view. You maintain one declaration.

The relationship to OpenAPI, MCP, and the other standards is covered question by question in the [FAQ](faq.md).

## Who is likely to benefit first

This is a hypothesis, not a finding. The most promising first users look like teams building interactive business applications, planning tools, and administrative workflows, where people and agents work on the same records and a wrong write is expensive. Those applications already have the logic, the permissions, and the approval steps; what they lack is one way to expose them to agents that behaves the same as the UI, can be inspected, and can be tested. Evaluation, operational visibility, and safe execution may matter more to them than the wire format. No pilot has run yet ([the pilot plan](pilot-plan.md) says how one would), and nothing here shows that such teams will adopt or pay for it; the [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md) lists what would test the hypothesis.

## When you should not use AXE yet

AXE wraps business logic that already works. If any of the following is true, wait.

- **No stable logic to wrap.** If the flow you would expose is still changing weekly, the manifest will churn with it and agents will learn not to trust it. Ship the flow first.
- **A purely informational site.** If agents only need to read your content, `llms.txt` or well-structured HTML serves them better than an action with no follow-up. AXE earns its keep when there is something to do.
- **Flows that must be human end to end.** Some steps are legally required to be performed by the person: certain signatures, attestations, and regulated disclosures. A manifest whose every action is a `needs_human` on the first call is honest but not useful. Expose the read actions around the flow and leave the flow alone.
- **You cannot commit to a secret and HTTPS.** Continuation and resume tokens are signed with a server `secret`, and `baseUrl` must be HTTPS outside localhost. If your deployment cannot keep a secret out of source control and serve TLS, agents will be handed tokens that anyone can forge.

Each of these is a precondition, not a permanent judgment about your site.

## Next steps

- [Getting started](getting-started.md): one read-only action, conformant, in about 15 minutes.
- [Concepts](concepts.md): the manifest, the result envelope, and the escalation ladder.
- [FAQ](faq.md): how AXE relates to MCP, OpenAPI, llms.txt, schema.org, and agent-to-agent protocols.
- [Evaluation](evaluation.md): what the scripted harness measures and what it does not.
- [Audit](audit.md): the AXE Score and the honesty rules in full.

# docs/getting-started.md

# Getting started

There are two ways in. If you have a web application and want a desktop agent to drive it through the controls people already use, start with the Surface and MCP-service steps below. If you want to declare server operations as typed actions an agent calls over HTTP, skip to [Serve actions over AXE](#serve-actions-over-axe).

## Add Surface to an existing app in four steps

Out of the box Surface discovers the page's controls and keeps their authoritative live state, revision, ledger, and handlers in the page. The browser relay client connects that Surface to the separately operated Agent Experience MCP service, so the consuming application does not run a server. WebMCP remains an additional direct path where supported, and development publishes `window.__surface`. It works with React Router 7 (framework mode), the Next.js App Router, Vite with React, React under any other bundler, and plain HTML pages.

### 1. Install

```sh
npm install @summationai/axe-surface @summationai/axe-relay
```

The packages come from the summationai GitHub Packages registry: an `.npmrc` beside `package.json` maps the scope (`@summationai:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com` and `//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}`), and `gh auth refresh -s read:packages && export NODE_AUTH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token)` supplies the token; see [Install from GitHub Packages](deploying.md#install-from-github-packages). Without registry access, `axe surface init --vendor <dir> --install` installs the `core`, `surface`, and `relay` tarballs packed with `scripts/pack-for-consumer.sh`, including the `overrides` (npm), `pnpm.overrides`, or root `resolutions` (Yarn) entry; see [Consume from a checkout](deploying.md#consume-from-a-checkout). Server dependencies remain in the provider-operated Agent Experience service.

### 2. Run `axe surface init`

```sh
npx @summationai/axe surface init --app-id acme-analytics --app-name "Acme Analytics" --dry-run
```

`axe surface init` detects the framework, the package manager (npm, pnpm, Yarn classic and Berry workspaces, bun), and the root component, and prints the diff it would make. For a React Router 7 app it is two lines in `app/root.tsx` plus two new files:

It is also the upgrade entry point: rerunning it applies narrowly defined safe migrations to files carrying its generated marker while preserving application-specific edits. Review the printed diff before accepting it.

```diff
 import "./app.css";
+import { AgentSurface } from "./surface";
@@
 export default function App() {
-  return <Outlet />;
+  return (
+    <AgentSurface>
+      <Outlet />
+    </AgentSurface>
+  );
 }
```

`app/surface.tsx` holds the `<AgentSurface>` component: a `SurfaceProvider` from `@summationai/axe-surface/react` with WebMCP enabled and an injected provider connection through `@summationai/axe-relay/client`. It is enabled by default; add an explicit `--flag` only when product rollout requires one. The generated structured profile publishes the stable application id and name plus live authentication/context facts. `app/surface.config.ts` is an empty overlay with commented examples. Nothing else in the app changes, and a second run changes nothing. Apply it:

```sh
npx @summationai/axe surface init --app-id acme-analytics --app-name "Acme Analytics" --yes
```

Options that matter on a real app:

- `--mount <file>`: mount in the highest application shell, including login and account/workspace selection routes. `init` lists the layouts it found.
- `--app-id` and `--app-name`: set the identity expected by the provider connector. Defaults are inferred from `package.json`; review them before applying.
- `--flag <NAME>`, `--flag <module>#<export>`, or `--flag-hook … --flag-import …`: deliberately gate Surface for a staged rollout. There is no flag by default.
- `--relay <url>`: connect a person's visible page to a company-operated relay when deliberately using the attended-tab shape.
- `--relay-dev`: connect a visible page to the loopback development relay and use code pairing as a diagnostic.
- `--browser-only`: omit the injected relay client and provide only browser-native WebMCP.

### 3. Register the application with the provider

The application team stops here. The provider adds a connector to its trusted registry with the application URL, allowed origins, identity claim mapping, and session strategy. It does not copy selectors, login steps, account names, or workflow instructions into MCP code. Those remain live Surface state.

For local provider development, set `AXE_CONNECTORS_FILE` and start the standalone service in the Agent Experience checkout—not in the consuming application:

```sh
AXE_CONNECTORS_FILE=./mcp/connectors.local.json pnpm mcp:hosted-dev
```

The public plugin names one stable provider `/mcp` endpoint. When a request names an application, the agent uses `apps_search` and `app_connect` when needed, then `relay_tabs`, `surface_read`, `surface_observe`, `surface_wait`, and the Surface action tools. One registered application is selected automatically. There is no application-owned MCP deployment or pairing step. See [`mcp/README.md`](../mcp/README.md).

Controls classified as high risk, controls that declare confirmation, and controls waiting on `approval_required` wait for the person through the active transport’s trusted approval channel: the agent client or a one-time approval page when unattended, and the page indicator when attended. An agent tool argument is never approval.

In a compatible browser, WebMCP also registers the same page-held Surface directly; use the [host preflight](webmcp.md#host-compatibility-and-preflight) when testing that optional path. In development, `window.__surface` remains available for diagnosis.

When an authenticated agent has no application session, the provider uses the selected connector's trusted session strategy or a one-time browser handoff. `injectedRelay()` recognizes the provider capability and connects automatically. The application adds no MCP server, token endpoint, session broker, or shared secret. See [ChatGPT consumer path](chatgpt-plugin.md).

### 4. Measure and refine

Run the coverage report and write config for the top gaps, or hand a coding agent the integration prompt:

```sh
npx @summationai/axe surface coverage http://localhost:5173 --routes /,/plans --out coverage.md
npx @summationai/axe surface prompt > integrate-surface.md
```

The report opens the app in headless Chromium through Playwright (install it with `npm install -D playwright && npx playwright install chromium` if it is not already there), calls `window.__surface.coverage()` on each page, and lists what the page could not say with the rule to paste for each. [Surface](surface.md) covers the model, and [Deploying](deploying.md) the rollout.

## Optional: direct one-application host development

To exercise the lower-level host directly instead of the provider registry:

```sh
npx @summationai/axe surface init --yes --install
npx @summationai/axe host login http://localhost:5173
claude mcp add myapp -- npx @summationai/axe host --dev --stdio --app http://localhost:5173
```

The host runs the app in a private browser and presents the surface over MCP. A brokered session may start it signed in; otherwise a `signed-out` Surface produces a secure view of that same browser for the person to authenticate without sending credentials through chat. The authoritative surface and every agent act remain in the page. This is useful for SDK development; production uses the provider registry and stable MCP endpoint described above. See [Unattended mode](host.md).

## Serve actions over AXE

In about 15 minutes you will install the SDK, expose one read-only action from an existing app, verify it with the conformance suite, and call it from Claude Desktop through MCP. Every command below is shown with the output you should see.

This tutorial uses a yoga studio. Nothing in it is specific to yoga; swap in your own domain as you go.

### Prerequisites

- Node 20 or newer.
- An existing Express, Next.js, or fetch-based app (Hono, Remix, Cloudflare Workers, Bun, Deno, SvelteKit). If you have none, the Express server below is complete on its own.

### 1. Install

```sh
npm install @summationai/axe-core @summationai/axe-express
npm install -D @summationai/axe tsx
```

Use `@summationai/axe-next` or `@summationai/axe-fetch` instead of `@summationai/axe-express` for those frameworks. The packages come from the summationai GitHub Packages registry: an `.npmrc` beside `package.json` maps the scope (`@summationai:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com` and `//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}`), and `gh auth refresh -s read:packages && export NODE_AUTH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token)` supplies the token; see [Install from GitHub Packages](deploying.md#install-from-github-packages). The `@summationai/axe` package is the CLI (its command is `axe`); `tsx` lets the CLI load your TypeScript directly.

### 2. Declare one action

Create `axe.ts`. It creates the server object and registers a single read-only action that wraps a function you already have (here, an in-memory list standing in for your database).

<!-- include: examples/getting-started/axe.ts#all -->
```ts
import { createAXE, action, z } from "@summationai/axe-core";

export const axe = createAXE({
  name: "Sunrise Yoga Studio",
  description:
    "Search upcoming yoga classes by date and style, see instructor names and spots left, and (once signed in) book or cancel a spot.",
  baseUrl: process.env.AXE_BASE_URL ?? "http://localhost:3000",
  humanFallbackUrl: "http://localhost:3000",
  auth: { modes: ["none"] },
  policies: { rateLimit: { requestsPerMinute: 60 }, termsUrl: "http://localhost:3000/terms" },
  contact: { email: "hello@sunriseyoga.example" },
  // Signs continuation and resume tokens. Set AXE_SECRET in production (docs/deploying.md).
  secret: process.env.AXE_SECRET ?? "development-only-secret-change-me",
});

const ClassSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  title: z.string(),
  style: z.enum(["vinyasa", "yin", "hatha"]),
  startsAt: z.string().datetime(),
  instructor: z.string(),
  spotsLeft: z.number().int(),
  url: z.string(),
});

// In a real integration this is your database or your existing service layer.
const CLASSES: z.infer<typeof ClassSchema>[] = [
  {
    id: "c_101",
    title: "Morning Vinyasa",
    style: "vinyasa",
    startsAt: "2026-10-01T14:00:00Z",
    instructor: "Priya N.",
    spotsLeft: 6,
    url: "http://localhost:3000/classes/c_101",
  },
  {
    id: "c_102",
    title: "Candlelight Yin",
    style: "yin",
    startsAt: "2026-10-01T03:00:00Z",
    instructor: "Marcus L.",
    spotsLeft: 2,
    url: "http://localhost:3000/classes/c_102",
  },
  {
    id: "c_103",
    title: "Hatha Basics",
    style: "hatha",
    startsAt: "2026-10-02T17:00:00Z",
    instructor: "Priya N.",
    spotsLeft: 10,
    url: "http://localhost:3000/classes/c_103",
  },
];

axe.register(
  action("classes.search", {
    title: "Search upcoming classes",
    description:
      "Find upcoming classes by date range and style. Returns up to 50 classes with start time, instructor, and spots left. Does not book anything.",
    readOnly: true,
    risk: "none",
    input: z.object({
      from: z.string().date().describe("Earliest class date, YYYY-MM-DD"),
      to: z.string().date().optional().describe("Latest class date, YYYY-MM-DD"),
      style: z.enum(["vinyasa", "yin", "hatha"]).optional().describe("Yoga style"),
    }),
    output: z.object({ classes: z.array(ClassSchema) }),
    display: {
      kind: "list",
      items: "/classes",
      item: {
        id: "/id",
        title: "/title",
        subtitle: "/instructor",
        url: "/url",
        attributes: [
          { label: "Starts", path: "/startsAt", format: "datetime", compare: "lower-better" },
          { label: "Style", path: "/style", format: "text" },
          { label: "Spots left", path: "/spotsLeft", format: "number", compare: "higher-better" },
        ],
      },
      suggestedComparison: ["Starts", "Spots left"],
      disclaimer:
        "Availability changes quickly. Confirm on the class page before planning around it.",
    },
    examples: [{ input: { from: "2026-10-01" }, output: { classes: CLASSES } }],
    handler: async ({ input }) => ({
      classes: CLASSES.filter(
        (c) =>
          c.startsAt.slice(0, 10) >= input.from &&
          (!input.to || c.startsAt.slice(0, 10) <= input.to) &&
          (!input.style || c.style === input.style),
      ),
    }),
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

Three things to notice:

- `description` is written for a model: what it does, what it returns, what it does not do. Agents choose actions by reading these. See [Designing actions](designing-actions.md#writing-descriptions).
- `display` tells agents which fields matter when a user compares classes, where the human page is, and what caveat must accompany any rendering. It is data about data, never markup. See [Presenting results](presenting-results.md).
- `examples` are real input/output pairs. They are validated against the schemas at registration and used by `axe conformance` and `axe audit` to exercise the action.

You can also scaffold this file with `axe init`, which asks for your framework and writes both `axe.ts` and the mount file.

### 3. Mount it

#### Express

<!-- include: examples/getting-started/server-express.ts#all -->
```ts
import express from "express";
import { axeExpress } from "@summationai/axe-express";
import { axe } from "./axe";

const app = express();

// Serves /.well-known/axe.json and every /axe/* endpoint. Everything else falls through.
// Mounted before any body parser, it reads its own request bodies within maxBodyBytes and
// answers an oversized one with an AXE envelope.
app.use(axeExpress(axe));
app.use(express.json());

app.get("/", (_req, res) => {
  res.send("Sunrise Yoga Studio");
});

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Listening on http://localhost:${port}`);
});
```
<!-- /include -->

Run it:

```sh
npx tsx server.ts
````

```
Listening on http://localhost:3000
```

#### Next.js (App Router)

Create `app/axe/[...axe]/route.ts` and `app/.well-known/axe.json/route.ts`, each with the same three exports:

<!-- include: examples/getting-started/route.ts#all -->
```ts
import { axeNext } from "@summationai/axe-next";
import { axe } from "./axe";

export const { GET, POST, OPTIONS } = axeNext(axe);
```

See [Next.js integration](integrations/next.md) for the Pages API and for passing your session into `context`.

#### Hono, Remix, Workers, Bun, Deno, SvelteKit

```ts
import { Hono } from "hono";

import { axeFetch } from "@summationai/axe-fetch";
import { axe } from "./axe";

const app = new Hono();

app.all("/axe/*", (c) => handler(c.req.raw));
app.get("/.well-known/axe.json", (c) => handler(c.req.raw));
app.get("/", (c) => c.text("Sunrise Yoga Studio"));

serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000) });
```

See [fetch integration](integrations/fetch.md) for each framework's exact mount.

### 4. Look at it the way an agent does

```sh

````

```

  Search upcoming yoga classes by date and style, see instructor names and spots left, and (once signed in) book or cancel a spot.
  manifest: http://localhost:3000/.well-known/axe.json (via well-known)
  baseUrl: http://localhost:3000   human site: http://localhost:3000

  classes.search  Search upcoming classes

    examples: 1

Affordance graph:
  entry points: classes.search
```

The manifest itself is plain JSON at `/.well-known/axe.json`. Any HTTP client can call the action with `fetch`:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/axe/actions/classes.search \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input":{"from":"2026-10-01","style":"yin"}}'
```

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "output": {
    "classes": [
      {
        "id": "c_102",
        "title": "Candlelight Yin",
        "style": "yin",
        "startsAt": "2026-10-01T03:00:00Z",
        "instructor": "Marcus L.",
        "spotsLeft": 2,
        "url": "http://localhost:3000/classes/c_102"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Every response is a result envelope with a `status`. The five statuses and when to return each are in [Concepts](concepts.md#the-result-envelope).

### 5. Validate and run conformance

`axe validate` loads your file, validates the manifest against the schema, and lints the agent-read text:

```sh
npx @summationai/axe validate ./axe.ts
```

```
./axe.ts exports `axe`: Sunrise Yoga Studio, 1 action(s)
✓ Manifest validates against the schema
  • classes.search — Search upcoming classes [read, risk none, auth none]
✓ No lint findings

0 error(s), 0 warning(s).
```

`axe conformance` runs the protocol suite against the live server. This is how you know you are done:

```sh
npx @summationai/axe conformance http://localhost:3000
```

```

PASS  discovery.alias                 Manifest also at /axe/manifest
PASS  discovery.headers               Manifest Content-Type and Cache-Control
PASS  runtime.protocol-header         AXE-Protocol header on the manifest
WARN  discovery.hints                 Discovery hint (robots.txt directive, link tag, or header)
                                      No AXE-Manifest line in robots.txt, no <link rel="axe-manifest">, no AXE-Manifest header on the home page. Optional, but it helps agents that start from a page URL.
PASS  manifest.schema                 Manifest validates against the schema
...
PASS  runtime.example-roundtrip       Read actions return ok for their examples; outputs validate; display resolves
...
36 passed, 0 failed, 1 warnings, 27 skipped. Conformant.
Skipped checks were not verified: "Conformant" means no check failed, not that every requirement was exercised. Each skip's detail line says what the run lacked.
...
```

The skipped checks exercise mutating actions and the escalation ladder; they run once you add a mutating action and pass `--auth`. Until then they are not verified, which is what the second line says. The one warning is a hint you can fix with a single line in `robots.txt`; see [Deploying](deploying.md#discovery).

`axe audit` gives you the AXE Score and a fix list, in the style of Lighthouse:

```sh
npx @summationai/axe audit http://localhost:3000
```

```
AXE Score: 88 / 100   http://localhost:3000/
...
Fix list (highest impact first):
 1. +9.2 Affordance graph is connected: reads lead somewhere, transactions are reachable [Actionable]
    classes.search returns a list but offers no affordances
    See docs/presenting-results.md#affordances
 2. +3.2 robots.txt directive, link tag, or header points at the manifest [Discoverable]
    Add "AXE-Manifest: <url>" to robots.txt or <link rel="axe-manifest"> to your pages.
    See docs/deploying.md#discovery
```

A single read action with no follow-up is a dead end for an agent; the next thing to add is a booking action and an affordance from each class to it. [Designing actions](designing-actions.md) walks through exactly that.

### 6. Connect Claude Desktop

The same declaration is an MCP server. Add this to Claude Desktop's `claude_desktop_config.json` (Settings → Developer → Edit Config):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sunrise-yoga": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "axe", "mcp", "http://localhost:3000"]
    }
  }
}
```

Restart Claude Desktop. It now has a `classes_search` tool (dots become underscores) whose description is your action's description. Ask it:

> What yin classes does Sunrise Yoga have on October 1st?

Claude calls `classes_search` with `{ "from": "2026-10-01", "style": "yin" }`, and because the action declares `display`, the tool result includes a comparison table with a link to each class alongside the raw JSON. For Claude Code, run `claude mcp add sunrise-yoga -- npx -y @summationai/axe mcp http://localhost:3000`. Details and the full mapping are in [MCP](mcp.md).

### What you have

- A manifest at `/.well-known/axe.json` that an AXE client can discover.
- One typed, described, presentable action at `/axe/actions/classes.search`.
- A passing conformance check (with the ladder checks skipped, so not yet verified) and an audit score with a fix list.
- An MCP server derived from the same declaration.

Everything from here is additive. You never have to change what you shipped today to add a booking action, a payment requirement, or a human handoff.

# docs/concepts.md

# Concepts

Everything in AXE is built from a dozen ideas. This page defines each one, shows the wire shape, and says when to use it. The normative text is the [protocol spec](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md); this page is the map.

Most of these ideas are about behavior, not the wire: a typed action with declared risk, a result that is one of five statuses, availability with a reason, a revision that makes a stale write fail, a handoff bound to the exact call. They hold whether an agent reaches your application over MCP, through WebMCP tools in a page, by reading the page, or as an AXE client. The manifest and the HTTP paths are how an AXE client sees them; the other interfaces carry the same actions and results in their own form ([MCP](mcp.md), [WebMCP](webmcp.md), [Surface](surface.md)).

## Manifest

The manifest is the document an agent reads first: who you are, what you can do, how to authenticate, and what the rules are. It is served at `/.well-known/axe.json` (and `/axe/manifest`), cached for a few minutes, and contains every action definition.

```json
{
  "protocol": "axe/0.1",
  "name": "Northgate University Admissions",
  "description": "Check application status, upload transcripts and recommendation letters, and schedule campus visits for prospective students.",
  "baseUrl": "https://admissions.northgate.example",
  "humanFallbackUrl": "https://admissions.northgate.example",
  "auth": {
    "modes": ["none", "user"],
    "userLoginUrl": "https://admissions.northgate.example/login"
  },
  "actions": [],
  "policies": {
    "rateLimit": { "requestsPerMinute": 60 },
    "termsUrl": "https://admissions.northgate.example/terms"
  },
  "contact": { "email": "agents@northgate.example" }
}
```

`description` is written for agents, not for a landing page: what this organization does and what an agent can accomplish here. `humanFallbackUrl` is where an agent sends the user when nothing else works. `policies` carries rate limits, terms, and an optional allow/deny list of agent vendors; `deny` wins.

In code you never write this JSON. `createAXE` takes the site-level fields and `describe` returns the manifest, with every registered action's schemas converted from Zod to JSON Schema.

## Action

An action is one thing an agent can do: a name, agent-facing text, an input schema, an output schema, safety metadata, and a handler. Names are namespaced kebab-case joined by dots: `applications.status`, `transcripts.upload`, `visits.schedule`.

<!-- include: examples/concepts/action.ts#action -->
```ts
axe.register(
  action("applications.status", {
    title: "Check application status",
    description:
      "Returns the current status of the signed-in applicant's admission application, the list of missing documents, and the decision date once released. Does not change anything.",
    readOnly: true,
    risk: "none",
    auth: "user",
    input: z.object({
      term: z
        .enum(["fall-2027", "spring-2027"])
        .optional()
        .describe("Admission term; defaults to the most recent application"),
    }),
    output: z.object({
      applicationId: z.string(),
      status: z.enum(["incomplete", "under-review", "decided"]),
      missingDocuments: z.array(z.string()),
      decisionDate: z.string().nullable(),
    }),
    examples: [
      {
        input: {},
        output: {
          applicationId: "NU-2027-0142",
          status: "incomplete",
          missingDocuments: ["transcript"],
          decisionDate: null,
        },
      },
    ],
    handler: async ({ input, context }) => admissions.status(context.onBehalfOf!, input.term),
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

The metadata is what makes an action safe to expose:

| Field        | Meaning                                                                                     |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `readOnly`   | Changes nothing. Read-only actions never need an idempotency key.                           |
| `idempotent` | Repeating with the same `idempotencyKey` has no additional effect.                          |
| `reversible` | The effect can be undone by the user or the site.                                           |
| `risk`       | `none`, `low`, `medium`, or `high`. Agents confirm with the user before high-risk actions.  |
| `auth`       | `none`, `site`, or `user`. See [Auth modes](#auth-modes).                                   |

Registration validates everything it can: the name pattern, that a mutating action is not `risk: "none"`, that examples validate against the schemas, that display pointers resolve, that affordances bind real inputs, and that no agent-read text contains instructions aimed at the agent. A bad definition throws with a message that names the field to fix, before any agent sees it.

## Display and affordances: the agent's map of the site

Most agent tasks start with a read: "find me a 1-bedroom in Bellevue under $3,200", "which yin classes are on Tuesday", "what is the status of my application". The agent then has to show the user something and let them pick.

`display` is how an action says which fields matter. It points into the output with RFC 6901 JSON Pointers: where the list is, which field is the id the agent echoes back, the title, the price, the attributes to compare, the human page to link to, the disclaimer that must accompany any rendering. It is a sibling of `output`, never a replacement, and entirely optional.

`affordances` are the follow-ups that make sense for each item, with inputs pre-bound by pointer: from a search result, "Schedule a tour" and "Apply for this unit"; from an order, "Start a return". They are declared statically on the action, so an agent knows the graph before calling anything, and can be overridden per item at runtime under the reserved `_axe` key when the set depends on state. At most one is `primary`.

<!-- include: examples/apartments/site.ts#display -->
```ts
display: {
  kind: "list",
  items: "/units",
  item: {
    id: "/id",
    title: "/name",
    subtitle: "/address",
    image: "/photos",
    url: "/humanUrl",
    price: { amount: "/rentUsd", currency: "USD", period: "month" },
    attributes: [
      { label: "Bedrooms", path: "/bedrooms", format: "number" },
      { label: "Bathrooms", path: "/bathrooms", format: "number" },
      { label: "Size", path: "/sqft", format: "area", compare: "higher-better" },
      { label: "Available", path: "/availableFrom", format: "date", compare: "lower-better" },
      { label: "Pets", path: "/petPolicy", format: "text" },
      { label: "Parking", path: "/parking", format: "text" },
    ],
    badges: ["/badges"],
  },
  suggestedComparison: ["Size", "Available", "Pets"],
  emptyMessage:
    "No units match those filters. Widening the rent ceiling or removing the move-in date usually helps.",
  disclaimer:
    "Pricing and availability change frequently. Confirm on the listing page before applying.",
},
```
<!-- /include -->

<!-- include: examples/apartments/site.ts#affordances -->
```ts
affordances: [
  { action: "tours.book", title: "Schedule a tour", input: { unitId: "/id" } },
  {
    action: "applications.submit",
    title: "Apply for this unit",
    input: { unitId: "/id" },
    primary: true,
  },
],
```
<!-- /include -->

The reference renderers in `@summationai/axe-client/present` turn a result plus its `display` into a Markdown table or a self-contained HTML page whose buttons dispatch the bound affordance. [Presenting results](presenting-results.md) covers the whole arc.

## The result envelope

Every response from an action, a continuation, a resume, or a poll is one JSON object with a `status`. Agents branch on `status`, never on the HTTP status.

| `status`      | Members                                                                          | Meaning                                                          |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ok`          | `output`                                                                         | Done.                                                            |
| `needs_input` | `reason`, `message`, `accepts`, `continuationToken`, `expiresAt`, `fallback`     | The agent may be able to supply what is missing.                 |
| `needs_human` | `handoff`                                                                        | The human must act on the site.                                  |
| `pending`     | `pollUrl`, `retryAfter`                                                          | Long-running work; poll later.                                   |
| `error`       | `error` with `code`, `message`, `retryable`, `details`                           | Failed.                                                          |

### Which to return when

| Situation                                                                                                     | Return        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| The work is done.                                                                                             | `ok`          |
| Something is missing that an agent could plausibly hold: a payment credential, a document, an address, a consent. | `needs_input`, with a `fallback` handoff if a human could also do it on the site |
| Only a human can do the next step: sign in person, complete a CAPTCHA the site insists on, pass legal review, log in where no credential pass-through exists. | `needs_human` |
| The result will take longer than a request should wait.                                                       | `pending`     |
| Input was wrong, the caller is not allowed, the entity does not exist, state conflicts, the server failed.   | `error`       |

In a handler you return the output value for `ok`, or one of the helpers: `needsInput`, `handoff`, `pending`, `fail`. Thrown exceptions become a generic `internal` error and go to the `onError` hook; nothing internal reaches the agent.

Error codes are a fixed set: `invalid_input`, `unauthorized`, `forbidden`, `not_found`, `conflict`, `rate_limited`, `unavailable`, `internal`, `unsupported`. For `invalid_input`, `details` carries `issues`, each with a JSON Pointer `path` and a `message`, so agents fix their own mistakes without bothering the user.

## The escalation ladder

The most important idea in the protocol. When an action cannot complete, the site's first move is to ask the agent for a specific thing; the human is the last resort.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Agent calls action] --> B{Can the site finish?}
  B -- yes --> OK[ok: output]
  B -- something is missing --> NI[needs_input: accepts list]
  B -- only a human can do it --> NH[needs_human: handoff]
  NI --> C{Agent holds a matching kind?}
  C -- yes, confirm if sensitive --> CONT[POST /axe/continue] --> B
  C -- no, fallback present --> NH
  C -- no, no fallback --> ASK[Agent asks its user, then continues] --> CONT
  NH --> H[Human acts on the site] --> RES[POST /axe/resume] --> B
````

Three rungs:

1. **Complete.** Return `ok`.
2. **Ask the agent.** Return `needs_input` with an ordered `accepts` list. Each entry names a `kind` (`payment.ach-debit`, `identity.government-id`, `document.url`, `consent.terms`, ...), a JSON Schema for the payload, and whether it is `sensitive`. An agent with a wallet or credential store fulfills it without involving the user beyond a confirmation.
3. **Hand off to the human.** Return `needs_human`, or attach a `fallback` handoff to a `needs_input` so an agent that can satisfy nothing goes straight to the human without another round trip.

The property manager example shows all three: submitting an application needs a deposit that can only be paid by ACH or wire (rung two, with two `accepts` and a `fallback`), and signing the lease requires an in-person signature (rung three).

<!-- include: examples/apartments/site.ts#submit-handler -->
```ts
handler: async ({ input, context, needsInput, handoff }) => {
  const app = await db.createApplication(input.unitId, context.onBehalfOf!);
  return needsInput({
    reason: "payment_required",
    message: `A refundable $${app.depositUsd} holding deposit is required to submit. Cards are not accepted.`,
    accepts: [
      accept(kinds.payment.achDebit, {
        description: "Authorize a one-time ACH debit for the deposit.",
      }),
      accept(kinds.payment.wireConfirmation, {
        description:
          "Provide the wire reference number after sending to the instructions below.",
        instructions: app.wireInstructions,
      }),
    ],
    state: { applicationId: app.id },
    // Only reached if the agent can satisfy neither option above.
    fallback: handoff({
      reason: "payment_required",
      instructions: "Pay the holding deposit by ACH or wire on the application page.",
      url: `https://oakridge-rentals.example/applications/${app.id}/deposit`,
      whatAgentShouldSayToUser:
        "Oakridge only takes the deposit by bank transfer, and I don't have bank details I can use for you. Can you complete it on their site? I'll finish the application once it's paid.",
      state: { applicationId: app.id },
    }),
  });
},
onContinue: async ({ kind, payload, state }) => {
  const { applicationId } = state as { applicationId: string };
  await payments.settleDeposit(applicationId, kind, payload);
  return db.submit(applicationId);
},
onResume: async ({ state }) => db.submit((state as { applicationId: string }).applicationId),
```
<!-- /include -->

## Requirements and kinds

A requirement is one `accepts` entry: a `kind`, a `title`, an agent-facing `description`, a `schema`, `sensitive`, and optional `instructions` the agent relays (wire details, where to obtain a document). Kinds are namespaced: the well-known registry in [`spec/KINDS.md`](../spec/KINDS.md) covers payment, identity, documents, contact, and consent; sites add their own under `x-<org>.<name>`.

Well-known kinds are what let an agent wallet fulfill a requirement automatically. `@summationai/axe-core/kinds` ships each one as a typed definition, and `accept` builds an entry from it, so a site writes `accept(kinds.payment.achDebit, { description })` instead of hand-rolling a schema. The server validates the submitted `payload` against the chosen entry's schema on `/axe/continue`; a failed validation returns `invalid_input` and does not consume the token. [Requirements and kinds](requirements-and-kinds.md) goes deep.

## Handoff and resume

A handoff is a structured request that the human do one thing on the site: a `reason`, `instructions` (what the human does), a `url` that lands on the step, a `resumeToken`, an `expiresAt`, and `whatAgentShouldSayToUser` (how the agent frames it). The SDK appends `axe_handoff=<id>` to the URL; the page at that URL can call `completeHandoff` when the human finishes, and `onResume` receives the original `state` plus whatever the page recorded.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant A as Agent
  participant X as AXE (site)
  participant S as Site UI
  A->>X: POST /axe/actions/applications.submit
  X-->>A: needs_input (accepts: ach-debit, wire) + fallback handoff
  alt Agent holds a matching kind
    A->>U: Confirm sending bank details?
    U-->>A: Yes
    A->>X: POST /axe/continue {kind, payload}
    X-->>A: ok
  else Nothing matches
    A->>U: whatAgentShouldSayToUser + url
    U->>S: Pays the deposit on the site
    S->>X: completeHandoff(id)
    A->>X: POST /axe/resume {resumeToken}
    X-->>A: ok
  end
````

Both tokens are signed, opaque to the agent, bound to the originating action, input, acting principal, and tenant, single-use, and expire (continuation tokens in about 15 minutes, resume tokens in about 24 hours). The `state` you attach never crosses the wire; it is stored server-side and delivered back to `onContinue` or `onResume`. [Human handoff](human-handoff.md) covers the landing page and failure modes.

## Idempotency

Every mutating action requires an `idempotencyKey` in the request envelope. Replaying a key with the same input, action, and principal within 24 hours returns the original result without running the handler; replaying it with different input returns `conflict`. The runtime claims the key atomically before the handler runs, so two simultaneous requests with one key run the handler once: the second gets a retryable `conflict` with `operationStatus` set to `in_progress` and a `Retry-After`, and its retry gets the stored result. Continuation and resume tokens work the same way: repeating a successful continue or resume returns its original envelope, so an agent whose response was lost recovers it. `@summationai/axe-client` generates a UUID per attempt automatically. The default store is in-memory; for more than one process use `SqliteIdempotencyStore` from `@summationai/axe-core/node` or implement `IdempotencyStore`, whose claim must be atomic ([Deploying](deploying.md#secrets-and-stores)). Idempotency makes the decision to run atomic, not your side effect: see [Operations, claims, and crashes](deploying.md#operations-claims-and-crashes).

## Live state and revisions

Idempotency keys make retries safe; they say nothing about a person and an agent editing the same record at the same time, or about which actions can be done right now. Two optional additions cover that. A site can publish a **revision**: one value that moves with every observable change, returned as `rev` on every envelope; an agent sends the revision it observed as `expectedRev`, and a call whose revision moved is refused with `conflict` (carrying `expectedRev` and `currentRev` in `details`) before anything runs. Each action can declare **availability**: whether it can be done right now and, if not, why, in the site's own words, with the kinds that would unblock it. The manifest carries the anonymous view under `live`; `/axe/state` serves the live, per-caller view uncached. [Live state and revisions](live-state.md) covers both; [Surface](surface.md) generates them from an application's own controls.

## Auth modes

| Mode   | Who authenticates | How                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------ | ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `none` | Nobody            | Public read-only actions.                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `site` | The agent         | `Authorization: Bearer <api-key>`; your `verifySiteKey` function says yes, no, or which actions the key may call.                                                                                                     |
| `user` | The end user      | Pass-through of a token the human already granted the agent (your `authenticate` function maps it to `onBehalfOf`), or a `login_required` handoff to your login page that binds the resume token to whoever signs in. |

The agent's claimed `onBehalfOf` in the request body is never trusted; handlers see the identity your code established. No OAuth server is built into v0; [Auth](auth.md) shows where one plugs in.

## Flows

A flow is a named, documented path through the affordance graph: `rent-a-unit` is `units.search` → `applications.submit` → `leases.sign`. Flows carry no server-side state and impose no order. They exist so agents and human readers of the manifest see the intended narrative, and so a site can group its actions. Affordances remain the primary chaining mechanism because they are local, stateless, and self-describing.

## Risk levels

| `risk`   | Use when                                                                                           |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `none`   | The action is read-only.                                                                           |
| `low`    | The effect is small and trivially reversed: save a search, join a waitlist, add a note.            |
| `medium` | The effect commits the user to something reversible at low cost: a booking with free cancellation. |
| `high`   | Money moves, a legal commitment is made, identity is asserted, or the effect is hard to reverse.   |

Agents use `risk` to decide how much to confirm with the user. Declaring it truthfully is part of the [honesty rules](audit.md#honesty-rules).

## Events

Every handled request emits one event: action, status, where on the ladder it landed, agent vendor, latency, tenant. No payloads, no identities. Sinks for console, JSON lines, and OpenTelemetry ship in `@summationai/axe-core/events`. [Analytics](analytics.md) has the day-one queries.

## Next steps

- [Designing actions](designing-actions.md): turning a human flow into actions, and writing descriptions a model can act on.
- [Presenting results](presenting-results.md): the search → present → select arc in full.
- [Protocol spec](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md): every rule, numbered.

# docs/surface.md

# Surface: live state for agents

The protocol in [Concepts](concepts.md) is outside-in: a site declares actions for the world's agents, with discovery, requirements, and handoff. Surface is the inside-out half: a running application publishes its live controls, with availability and reasons, under one revision, and an agent acts through the application's own handlers. `@summationai/axe-surface` implements it and `@summationai/axe-surface/axe` serves any surface as an AXE manifest, so the two halves share kinds, risk metadata, the result envelope, and the ladder. The normative text is [`spec/SURFACE.md`](../spec/SURFACE.md).

## Why a second shape

Hand-written actions beside a human UI drift the first time a button changes, and a static manifest cannot say what can be done right now. Surface came out of two trials on business applications: a draft board whose state lives in the browser, and a planning grid whose state lives on a server with a protected mutation protocol. In both, the agent view came out of the same components and handlers the humans use, so drift is impossible rather than detected, the agent knows why a control is unavailable before it tries, and a person and an agent can work on the same application at once because every act carries the revision the agent saw.

Three rules are the whole design:

1. **Surface reports; it never decides.** Availability is whatever the application computed to disable its own control.
2. **Same door.** An act runs the control's own handler, so authorization, validation, and persistence stay where they are.
3. **One revision.** Every observation carries it, every act presents it, and a stale act applies nothing.

## Application profile

A Surface may publish structured live identity and context beside its controls:

```ts
const surface = createSurface({
  profile: () => ({
    id: "example-app",
    name: "Example App",
    authentication: { state: signedIn ? "signed-in" : "signed-out" },
    context: workspace
      ? { kind: "workspace", id: workspace.id, name: workspace.name }
      : { kind: "workspace" },
  }),
});
```

The provider connector’s expected `surfaceId` must match `profile.id`. Authentication and context are facts from the running page and may change between observations. The profile contains no URLs, origins, OAuth, session policy, secrets, or agent-instruction field; those are provider-registry concerns. `setProfile` replaces or clears it, and `configure({ profile })` does the same for adapters.

## Registering controls

Every control that matters registers one entry: a stable `id`, a `kind` (`action`, `field`, or `collection`), a `role`, a `name` that states the outcome, the `object` it belongs to, its `state`, its `effect`, and the handler the control itself calls.

<!-- include: examples/surface/board.ts#create -->
```ts
import { createSurface } from "@summationai/axe-surface";

export const surface = createSurface({ app: "fantasy-draft" });
```
<!-- /include -->

<!-- include: examples/surface/board.ts#register -->
```ts
interface Player {
  id: string;
  player: string;
  pos: string;
}

export function registerRow(
  p: Player,
  ctx: {
    drafting: boolean;
    drafted: Record<string, "me" | "other">;
    seatable: boolean;
    takeMine: (p: Player, actor: string) => void;
  },
) {
  const taken = !!ctx.drafted[p.id];
  const takenBy = ctx.drafted[p.id] === "me" ? "you" : "another team";
  surface.register({
    id: `pick:me:${p.id}`,
    kind: "action",
    role: "button",
    name: `Draft ${p.player} (${p.pos})`,
    object: `player:${p.id}`,
    // Availability mirrors the button's own disabled logic, in the app's own words.
    state: !ctx.drafting
      ? { available: false, reason: "draft not started" }
      : taken
        ? { available: false, reason: `already drafted by ${takenBy}` }
        : !ctx.seatable
          ? { available: false, reason: `no roster slot left for a ${p.pos}` }
          : { available: true },
    effect: { mutates: "draft", idempotent: false, reversible: true, risk: "medium" },
    handler: (actor) => ctx.takeMine(p, actor),
  });
}
```
<!-- /include -->

`effect` is AXE's risk metadata: `mutates` names the state that changes, and `idempotent`, `reversible`, and `risk` mean what they mean on an [action](designing-actions.md#choosing-risk). `confirm` makes the act require explicit confirmation; `text` is the prompt for free text the handler takes ("reason for the lock").

Fields register a `value` and an `edit` descriptor (read-only with a reason, or editable with a `maxLength` and an optional `schema`). The schema is a JSON Schema for the text, or a Zod schema: the surface validates a Zod schema by calling its `safeParse` and never imports Zod itself, so a browser bundle of `@summationai/axe-surface` carries none. To publish a Zod schema in `observe()` the surface needs a converter: pass `toJsonSchema` from `@summationai/axe-core` as `createSurface({ toJsonSchema })` (or `configure({ toJsonSchema })`); registering a Zod schema without one throws with that instruction. The same converter renders the `requires` schemas below, which `accept()` from `@summationai/axe-core/kinds` builds with Zod. A JSON Schema needs nothing. Collections register `total`, `loaded`, `filter`, and `sort`, and are actionable when they can load more.

Each of them also receives the act's context as its last argument (`ActContext`: the entry `id`, the `op`, the `expectedRev` the agent presented, and the `actor`), for a write that has to carry the revision; see [Writing under a precondition](#writing-under-a-precondition). A handler, a field's `set`, or a collection's `more` may return `{ changed, rev }` (or a promise of it): `changed` names the entries the act moved and `rev` is the application's revision after the change. The surface folds both into the act result and the ledger. An application that bumps the revision itself can return nothing: `changed` is then the entry when the revision moved during the handler.

## The revision

The revision has one owner at a time. When state lives in the browser, the surface owns the counter: call `bump` after every change an agent could observe, whoever made it, and `seedRev` from persisted state on load. When the server already has a revision, the application owns it: adopt it with `setRev`, and the surface's stale check is the first of two, the server refusing a stale expected revision again. The surface remembers which it is (`revisionMode()`, `surface` or `app`) from the last of `bump` and `setRev`, or you pin it with `createSurface({ revision: "app" })`. The mode decides what a freeze does to the revision ([Transient states](#transient-states)); everything else is the same in both.

<!-- include: examples/surface/board.ts#revision -->
```ts
// State lives in the browser, so the app owns the counter: bump after every change an agent could
// observe, whoever made it, and expose observe/act for browser agents.
export function afterDraftChange(): void {
  surface.bump({ what: "draft" });
}
surface.expose(typeof window !== "undefined" ? window : null);
```
<!-- /include -->

`expose` publishes `observe`, `act`, `ledger`, and `rev` on the page for browser-driving agents. It is browser-local: anything running in the page can already read what the page shows and call its handlers, so `expose` gives no one access they did not have, and it needs no auth. Serving the same surface over HTTP is different; see [Who can observe and act](#who-can-observe-and-act). The names those agents read on the page come from the same entries; see [Accessible names](#accessible-names). In the first trial, two of three gains came from the names alone.

In a browser with WebMCP, the page can also offer the same controls to the browser's own agent as tools: use `<SurfaceProvider webMcp>` in React, or `exposeWebMcp(surface)` from `@summationai/axe-surface/webmcp` directly. Both register nothing where the browser has no WebMCP. See [WebMCP](webmcp.md).

## Observe and act

`observe` returns the live table: every entry with its `index` (a position among the rows that can be acted on now, `null` otherwise), its `state` with a `reason` when unavailable, its `effect`, current `value` for fields, plus `objects` the application chooses to show and the `rev`.

`act` takes `op`, `target` (the entry id, or its index at the same rev), optional `text` and `confirm`, and the `expectedRev` the agent observed. It returns the [result envelope](concepts.md#the-result-envelope): `ok` with `{ rev, id, actor, changed, seq }`, or `error` with `conflict` when the revision moved (nothing applied), `not_found` for an unknown target, `invalid_input` for a wrong op, missing confirm, or text that fails `maxLength` or the field's schema, and `unavailable` with the reason for a control the application has disabled. `changed` is what the handler reported, or the entry itself when the revision moved during the handler; for an application whose revision arrives from the server after the handler it is empty unless the handler reports it, so an agent re-observes rather than reading `changed` as the whole story. A `target` must be a non-empty id or a non-negative integer index; anything else (`null`, a fraction, a boolean) is `invalid_input` before any lookup, an index only ever resolves to the row that carried it at `expectedRev` and never to a row without one, and an id that names a disabled control is `unavailable` with its reason rather than `not_found`.

<!-- include: examples/surface/agent.ts#loop -->
```ts
import type { Surface } from "@summationai/axe-surface";

export async function draftBestAvailable(
  surface: Surface,
  prefer: (names: string[]) => string | undefined,
): Promise<string> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt++) {
    const view = surface.observe();
    const choices = view.entries.filter(
      (e) => e.kind === "action" && e.index !== null && e.id.startsWith("pick:me:"),
    );
    const name = prefer(choices.map((e) => e.name));
    const chosen = choices.find((e) => e.name === name);
    if (!chosen) return "nothing to draft";
    const result = await surface.act({
      op: "CLICK",
      target: chosen.id,
      expectedRev: view.rev,
      actor: "agent",
    });
    if (result.status === "ok") return `drafted ${chosen.name} at rev ${result.output.rev}`;
    // Someone else moved first: the act applied nothing. Look again.
    if (result.error.code === "conflict") continue;
    return `refused: ${result.error.message}`;
  }
  return "the board kept changing; gave up";
}
```
<!-- /include -->

Acts on one surface run one at a time, in the order `act` was called. Every check above runs when `act` is called, so a refusal comes back at once, even while another act's handler is still running. An act that passes them while another is in flight waits its turn, and when it reaches execution the surface checks it again: if the act ahead of it moved the revision, or a person did (`bump`, `setRev`), it is `conflict`; if the application froze in the meantime, or the control became unavailable, it is `unavailable`; in every case its handler does not run. So two acts presenting the same `expectedRev` cannot both commit when the first one moves the revision, and an act presenting a revision that a predecessor has since moved is `conflict`, as a retry after a lost response is. `observe`, `availability`, and `ledger` never wait: while a handler runs they report the state before it commits.

Two participants on one application collide safely: a human change between the agent's observe and act is caught as `conflict`; a retried act after a lost response is refused because the revision moved; an index that shifted cannot land on the row that slid into the slot; two acts from one observation are ordered and the second is checked against the first one's result. The tests in `packages/surface/test` pin each of those.

## Writing under a precondition

The surface's checks guard one surface. Two tabs of a server-state application each have their own surface, and both can pass their own check at the same revision; no queue in a browser can order writes on a server. There the write itself has to be the gate: the handler takes the `expectedRev` from its context and passes it into the transaction or conditional write, and when the write finds a newer revision it refuses. It refuses by throwing a `SurfaceConflict` (with the server's `currentRev` when it knows it) or by returning `{ conflict: { currentRev } }`. The surface returns `conflict` with `expectedRev` and `currentRev` in `details`, records a refusal in the ledger, and adopts nothing from the handler: the application's newer revision arrives the way it always does, through `setRev` on the next refresh. A handler that refuses must have written nothing.

<!-- include: examples/surface/precondition.ts#precondition -->
```ts
import { createSurface, SurfaceConflict } from "@summationai/axe-surface";

interface Plan {
  revision: number;
  cells: Record<string, string>;
}

// Stands in for the server: one branch revision, and a write that applies only at the expected
// revision (UPDATE ... SET value = $1, revision = revision + 1 WHERE revision = $expected).
const server: Plan = { revision: 129, cells: {} };
async function writeCell(id: string, value: string, expected: number): Promise<number | null> {
  if (server.revision !== expected) return null;
  server.cells[id] = value;
  server.revision += 1;
  return server.revision;
}

export const surface = createSurface({ app: "planning-app", revision: "app" });
surface.setRev(server.revision);

surface.register({
  id: "cell:demand:2026-03",
  kind: "field",
  role: "textbox",
  name: "Demand, March 2026",
  edit: {
    maxLength: 40,
    // The third argument is the act's context: the entry id and the expectedRev it presented.
    set: async (text, _actor, { id, expectedRev }) => {
      const rev = await writeCell(id, text, expectedRev);
      if (rev === null)
        throw new SurfaceConflict("The plan changed on the server.", {
          currentRev: server.revision,
        });
      // Report what changed and the revision the write produced; the surface adopts it.
      return { changed: [id], rev };
    },
  },
});
```
<!-- /include -->

To the caller, both gates look the same: `conflict`, nothing applied, observe again.

<!-- include: examples/surface/precondition.ts#outcome -->
```ts
export async function typeDemand(text: string): Promise<string> {
  const view = surface.observe();
  const result = await surface.act({
    op: "TYPE_TEXT",
    target: "cell:demand:2026-03",
    text,
    expectedRev: view.rev,
  });
  if (result.status === "ok") return `saved at rev ${result.output.rev}`;
  // Refused by the surface (another act or a person moved first) or by the server's write:
  // either way nothing was applied, and the ledger records a conflict.
  if (result.error.code === "conflict") return "someone moved first; observe again";
  return result.error.message;
}
```
<!-- /include -->

Three more rules keep the revision honest when handlers are asynchronous:

- A commit whose revision arrives later (the handler reports no `rev`, so the revision has not moved yet) still closes the acts that were waiting behind it at that revision: they are `conflict`, with a message saying the application has not reported its new revision. An agent that observes again and acts is accepted, so nothing waits on a revision that may never move. A handler that returns `changed: []` said it changed nothing, and the next act runs.
- A `rev` a handler reports that is older than the surface's revision when it settles (a newer one arrived with `setRev` while it ran) is not adopted. The act is still `ok`, `output.rev` is the current revision, and the ledger entry carries the report as `ignoredRev`.
- A handler that never settles holds back every later act, and a handler must not await an `act` on its own surface, which would wait for itself.

Per-entry revisions are not part of the contract: one revision per application is what the trials needed, and the server's conditional write can be as fine-grained as the application's own data model. See `DECISIONS.md`.

## Transient states

Availability is only as current as the last registration. Re-register an entry (or `reconcile`) whenever anything that feeds its `state`, `value`, or `edit` changes, and that includes transient states: a save in flight, data loading, a modal open. The first staging trial found a grid that disabled its cells during a save while the surface still reported them editable, and an agent typed into the frozen UI. For a state that spans the whole surface, `freeze(reason)` does it in one call: every entry reports unavailable with that reason, fields go read-only, no row carries an index, `observe` carries a top-level `frozen: { reason }`, acts return `unavailable` with the reason, and `onChange` listeners hear about the freeze and the `thaw`. Freezes nest; the surface thaws when the last one is released.

What a freeze does to the revision follows the [revision mode](#the-revision). When the surface owns it, `freeze` and `thaw` each move it, so an act planned before the freeze is `conflict`. When the application owns it, neither moves it: a freeze is not a change of the application's state, and a counter the surface moved on its own would run ahead of the server's until the next `setRev`, refusing agents for a change that never happened. An act planned before the freeze is then `unavailable` while frozen and accepted after the thaw exactly when the application's revision did not move.

<!-- include: examples/surface/save.ts#freeze -->
```ts
import { surface } from "./board";

export async function save(persist: () => Promise<void>): Promise<void> {
  const thaw = surface.freeze("saving");
  try {
    await persist();
  } finally {
    thaw();
  }
}
```
<!-- /include -->

## The ledger

The ledger is the application's one history, in memory, oldest first. It holds three things and nothing else:

- **Acts through the surface, run or refused.** Every call to `act` writes exactly one entry: `{ seq, at, op, target, actor, revBefore, revAfter, status, changed }`, with the `text` it carried under the text policy ([Sensitive values and the ledger's text](#sensitive-values-and-the-ledgers-text)). A refusal has an error code as its `status`, an empty `changed`, and `revAfter` equal to `revBefore`. Every act result carries its entry's `seq`.
- **Changes the application recorded itself**, marked `source: "application"`. A change made outside `act` (a person's own control that is not a registered entry, an approval, a push from the server) moves the revision but writes no entry, so an agent reading the ledger would find a revision it cannot account for. `record` appends one.
- **Calls the server refused before the surface**, marked `source: "server"`, when the surface is served through the bridge ([Serving a surface](#serving-a-surface-as-an-axe-manifest)): a stale `expectedRev`, refused by the protocol before the handler runs, is recorded as `conflict` with the entry id, the op, the caller as `actor`, and the `expectedRev` the caller presented.

`ledger({ since })` returns what came after a `ledgerSeq` an agent observed; `actor` filters and `limit` caps. Entries `act` writes carry no `source`.

<!-- include: examples/surface/ledger.ts#ledger -->
```ts
import { surface } from "./board";

// After observe() returned { rev, ledgerSeq }, an agent asks what happened after that snapshot.
export function whatHappenedSince(ledgerSeq: number): string[] {
  return surface
    .ledger({ since: ledgerSeq })
    .map((e) =>
      e.status === "ok"
        ? `#${e.seq} ${e.actor} ${e.op} ${e.target} (rev ${e.revBefore} -> ${e.revAfter})`
        : `#${e.seq} ${e.actor} ${e.op} ${e.target}: refused, ${e.status}, nothing applied`,
    );
}

// The person's view of the agent's work: newest twenty entries by the agent.
export function agentActivity() {
  return surface.ledger({ actor: "agent", limit: 20 });
}
```
<!-- /include -->

`record({ op, target, actor, changed?, text?, revBefore?, status? })` runs no handler and does not move the revision: the application makes its change and moves the revision (`bump`, `setRev`), then records it, passing the revision it read before as `revBefore` so the entry spans the move. `revAfter` is the revision when `record` is called; `op` is the application's own word (`APPROVE`, `UNDO`), not limited to the ops of `act`. The text policy and the sensitive rule apply as they do to an act. A refusal the surface never saw is recorded with an error code as `status` and `changed: []`; both revisions are then the current one.

<!-- include: examples/surface/ledger.ts#record -->
```ts
// The commissioner undoes a pick from the page's own admin menu, which is not a registered control,
// so the change never passes through act. Make the change, move the revision, then record it with
// the revision read before, so the entry spans the move and the ledger has no gap.
export function undoPickFromAdminMenu(playerId: string, undo: () => void): void {
  const revBefore = surface.currentRev();
  undo();
  surface.bump({ what: `undo:${playerId}` });
  surface.record({
    op: "UNDO",
    target: `pick:me:${playerId}`,
    actor: "commissioner",
    changed: [`pick:me:${playerId}`],
    revBefore,
  });
}
// The entry: { op: "UNDO", actor: "commissioner", revBefore: 7, revAfter: 8, status: "ok",
// source: "application", ... }. record runs no handler and does not move the revision itself.
```
<!-- /include -->

The ledger holds nothing else. A call the runtime refuses for a caller it did not admit (no credentials on a protected surface, a site key outside its allowlist), or before it knew the caller or the action (a malformed envelope, an oversized body), is only in the server's request events. Retention is bounded (`createSurface({ ledger: { max } })`, default 1000 entries); for a durable trail, sink the action events below, or the application's own store.

## Saying what would unblock a control

An unavailable action can declare `requires`, the same `accepts` list an AXE `needs_input` carries, with a `fulfill` the application runs when an agent supplies one of the kinds; and a `handoff` for a step only a human can take. A handoff has a `url` when a page names the step; when the step is taken inside the application itself (unlock a version from a menu) there is no page, so leave `url` out rather than invent one. Standalone, `act` reports both in `error.details`. Through the AXE bridge they become the ladder, except that a handoff without a `url` cannot become `needs_human` (there is nowhere to resume from) and stays an `unavailable` error whose `details.handoff` still says what would unblock the control.

<!-- include: examples/surface/requires.ts#lock -->
```ts
import { createSurface } from "@summationai/axe-surface";
import { toJsonSchema } from "@summationai/axe-core";
import { kinds, accept } from "@summationai/axe-core/kinds";

const plan = { approved: false, locked: false, revision: 129 };
// The server owns the revision (adopted as is with setRev), and the kinds below carry Zod
```
