- `kinds` is the registry as typed definitions grouped by namespace: `kinds.document.url`, `kinds.consent.terms`, and so on. Each definition carries the wire name, a title, a description, a Zod schema, and the default `sensitive`.
- `accept` builds an `accepts` entry from a definition. Pass `description` (what this requirement is for here), and optionally `title`, `instructions`, and `sensitive: true`.
- **withMimeTypes** restricts a document kind to specific MIME types by tightening `mimeType` to an enum. The result is a restriction of the registry schema, which the spec permits.
- **customKind** defines a kind under your own namespace. The name must be `x-<org>.<name>`; anything else throws.

Northgate admissions accepts a transcript by URL or inline, PDF only, and treats both as sensitive:

<!-- include: examples/requirements-and-kinds/transcript.ts#imports -->
```ts
import { createAXE, action, z } from "@summationai/axe-core";
import { kinds, accept, withMimeTypes } from "@summationai/axe-core/kinds";
```
<!-- /include -->

<!-- include: examples/requirements-and-kinds/transcript.ts#action -->
```ts
axe.register(
  action("transcripts.upload", {
    title: "Upload a transcript",
    description:
      "Attaches an official transcript to the signed-in applicant's application. Accepts a PDF by URL or as an inline upload of at most 10 MB. Returns the document id and the updated list of missing documents.",
    risk: "low",
    idempotent: true,
    reversible: true,
    auth: "user",
    input: z
      .object({
        issuingSchool: z.string().describe("Name of the school that issued the transcript"),
      })
      .strict(),
    output: z.object({ documentId: z.string(), missingDocuments: z.array(z.string()) }),
    handler: async ({ input, context, needsInput }) =>
      needsInput({
        reason: "document_required",
        message: `Provide the official transcript from ${input.issuingSchool} as a PDF.`,
        accepts: [
          // Most automatable first: an agent that already holds the file at a URL needs no encoding step.
          accept(withMimeTypes(kinds.document.url, ["application/pdf"]), {
            description:
              "An HTTPS URL to the transcript PDF. Northgate fetches it once, within 15 minutes of this response.",
            sensitive: true,
          }),
          accept(withMimeTypes(kinds.document.base64, ["application/pdf"]), {
            description: "The transcript PDF inline, at most 10 MB before base64 encoding.",
            sensitive: true,
          }),
        ],
        // Delivered to onContinue. Never sent to the agent.
        state: { applicantId: context.onBehalfOf!, issuingSchool: input.issuingSchool },
      }),
    onContinue: async ({ kind, payload, state, fail }) => {
      const { applicantId, issuingSchool } = state as {
        applicantId: string;
        issuingSchool: string;
      };
      // The payload already validated against the chosen entry's schema; the casts only name the shape.
      const file =
        kind === "document.url"
          ? await fetchDocument(payload as { url: string; mimeType: string })
          : decodeDocument(payload as { mimeType: string; contentBase64: string });
      if (file.bytes.byteLength > MAX_TRANSCRIPT_BYTES) {
        // An error from onContinue does not consume the token; the agent can retry with a smaller file.
        return fail("invalid_input", "The transcript is larger than 10 MB.", {
          issues: [
            {
              path: "/payload",
              message: "decoded size exceeds 10 MB",
              expected: "at most 10485760 bytes",
            },
          ],
        });
      }
      const documentId = await documents.store(applicantId, issuingSchool, file);
      return { documentId, missingDocuments: await documents.missing(applicantId) };
    },
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

Three things to notice. The `state` object carries the applicant id and the school from the first call into `onContinue` without ever reaching the agent. The `payload` arrives already validated against the chosen entry's schema, so the casts only name the shape. And a `fail` from `onContinue` leaves the token usable, so the agent can retry with a smaller file.

Sunrise Yoga's booking action shows the two most common `reason` codes on one action. A student who has not acknowledged the current liability waiver gets `consent_required`; a student without a membership gets `payment_required`. Both `accepts` are one entry long because each requirement has one natural shape:

<!-- include: examples/requirements-and-kinds/waiver.ts#waiver -->
```ts
const WAIVER = {
  url: "https://sunriseyoga.example/policies/liability-waiver",
  version: "2026-03",
  scope: "class-attendance-liability",
};

// The registry schema, tightened to this exact policy. The server then rejects a consent
// for any other document or version at validation time (spec [K-3], [P-HON-6]).
const waiverConsent: AcceptInput = {
  kind: kinds.consent.terms.kind,
  title: "Liability waiver",
  description: `Acknowledge the Sunrise Yoga liability waiver, version ${WAIVER.version}, for class attendance.`,
  schema: kinds.consent.terms.schema
    .extend({
      policyUrl: z.enum([WAIVER.url]),
      policyVersion: z.enum([WAIVER.version]),
      scope: z.enum([WAIVER.scope]),
    })
    .strict(),
  sensitive: false,
  instructions: `Liability waiver: the student confirms they are able to participate and releases Sunrise Yoga from liability for ordinary injuries during class. Full text at ${WAIVER.url}.`,
};
```
<!-- /include -->

<!-- include: examples/requirements-and-kinds/waiver.ts#action -->
```ts
axe.register(
  action("classes.book", {
    title: "Book a spot in a class",
    description:
      "Reserves one spot in a class for the signed-in student. First-time students acknowledge the liability waiver; students without a membership pay the drop-in rate. Returns the booking id. Cancellation is free up to 12 hours before the class.",
    risk: "medium",
    idempotent: true,
    reversible: true,
    auth: "user",
    input: z.object({ classId: z.string().describe("Class id from classes.search") }).strict(),
    output: z.object({ bookingId: z.string(), classId: z.string() }),
    handler: async ({ input, context }) => nextStep(input.classId, context.onBehalfOf!),
    onContinue: async ({ kind, payload, state }) => {
      const { classId, studentId } = state as { classId: string; studentId: string };
      if (kind === "consent.terms") {
        await students.recordWaiver(
          studentId,
          payload as { policyVersion: string; acceptedAt: string },
        );
      } else if (kind === "payment.card") {
        await payments.chargeDropIn(
          studentId,
          classId,
          payload as { token: string; provider: string },
        );
      }
      return nextStep(classId, studentId);
    },
  }),
);

async function nextStep(classId: string, studentId: string) {
  const student = await students.get(studentId);
  const cls = await classes.get(classId);
  if (student.waiverVersion !== WAIVER.version) {
    return needsInput({
      reason: "consent_required",
      message:
        "Sunrise Yoga requires an acknowledged liability waiver before a first class, and again when the waiver changes.",
      accepts: [waiverConsent],
      state: { classId, studentId },
    });
  }
  if (!student.hasMembership && !(await payments.hasPaid(studentId, classId))) {
    return needsInput({
      reason: "payment_required",
      message: `The drop-in rate for this class is $${cls.dropInUsd}. Members attend at no charge.`,
      accepts: [
        accept(kinds.payment.card, {
          description: `Card token to charge $${cls.dropInUsd} for one drop-in class.`,
        }),
      ],
      state: { classId, studentId },
    });
  }
  return classes.book(classId, studentId);
}
```
<!-- /include -->

The waiver entry is built by hand rather than with `accept` so that the schema pins `policyUrl`, `policyVersion`, and `scope` to the exact policy. A consent for any other document fails validation on `/axe/continue` before your code runs. That is what the consent scope rule asks for, enforced by the schema rather than by a check you might forget.

## How agents fulfill kinds

An agent that supports AXE can hold a wallet and a credential store keyed by kind; this is the design the client supports, not a description of agents that exist today. When a `needs_input` arrives, it walks `accepts` in order and asks each store whether it can produce a payload for that kind. `@summationai/axe-client` models this as a `Fulfiller`: a list of kinds and a function that returns a payload or nothing. The client's `run` drives the whole ladder: invoke, try each `accepts` entry against the registered `fulfillers`, call `/axe/continue`, follow a further `needs_input`, poll `pending`, and surface a handoff only when nothing else works.

Before any payload for an entry marked `sensitive` is sent, the client calls its `confirm` callback with the action, the entry, the payload, and your `message`. The agent shows the user a summary ("Oakridge needs a $500 refundable deposit by bank transfer. Use your checking account ending 4471?") and sends only on a yes. A client with no `confirm` skips sensitive options entirely, which is why a requirement that offers only sensitive kinds should carry a `fallback`.

This is also why `description` and `instructions` matter: they are what the agent reads aloud. [For agent builders](for-agent-builders.md) covers the client side in full.

## Custom kinds

A custom kind is legitimate when nothing in the registry describes the payload: a guarantor agreement, a pet's vaccination record, a purchase order in a format your ERP dictates. Oakridge Rentals needs a guarantor for some applicants:

<!-- include: examples/requirements-and-kinds/custom.ts#kind -->
```ts
// Nothing in the registry describes a guarantor agreement, so it is a custom kind.
// A custom kind that merely renamed payment.card or contact.address would be a fake kind ([P-HON-5]).
export const guarantorForm = customKind({
  kind: "x-oakridge.guarantor-form",
  title: "Guarantor agreement",
  description:
    "Who guarantees the lease, their relationship to the applicant, and the signed Oakridge guarantor form.",
  schema: z
    .object({
      guarantorName: z.string().min(1),
      relationship: z.enum(["parent", "guardian", "employer", "other"]),
      annualIncomeUsd: z.number().int().nonnegative(),
      signedFormUrl: z.string().url().describe("HTTPS URL of the signed guarantor form, PDF"),
    })
    .strict(),
  sensitive: true,
});
```
<!-- /include -->

<!-- include: examples/requirements-and-kinds/custom.ts#use -->
```ts
export function guarantorRequired(applicationId: string, rentUsd: number) {
  return needsInput({
    reason: "guarantor_required",
    message: `Applicants with verified income under three times the rent ($${rentUsd * 3}/month) need a guarantor.`,
    accepts: [
      accept(guarantorForm, {
        instructions:
          "Download the guarantor form at https://oakridge-rentals.example/forms/guarantor.pdf, have the guarantor sign it, and provide a URL Oakridge can fetch the signed PDF from.",
      }),
    ],
    state: { applicationId },
  });
}
```
<!-- /include -->

Three rules apply:

1. **Naming.** Custom kinds are `x-<org>.<name>`, kebab-case. customKind throws otherwise, and the well-known namespaces are closed to sites.
2. **No fake kinds.** A custom kind whose schema is structurally equivalent to a well-known kind's schema is a hard failure in `axe audit` and the conformance suite (spec [P-HON-5]). Renaming `payment.card` to `x-yourorg.card` does not give you anything; it forces every agent that holds a card token into a handoff it did not need.
3. **Consent scope.** A `consent.terms` requirement must name the exact `policyUrl`, `policyVersion`, and `scope` the action needs, and must not bundle consent for unrelated purposes (spec [P-HON-6]). If you need two consents, return two requirements, as the chaining section shows.

Expect agents to need a human for a custom kind more often than for a well-known one, since no wallet is pre-populated with it. Give the entry `instructions` that tell the agent exactly where to obtain the thing, and attach a `fallback` so a human can do it on your site.

## Validation on `/axe/continue`

The agent posts `{ continuationToken, kind, payload }`. The server:

1. Verifies the token's signature, expiry, binding, and tenant, and re-establishes the acting principal: the same user, the same site key (verified again), or none, exactly as when the token was minted. A tampered, expired, wrong-tenant, or wrong-principal token is `not_found`; the response does not say which.
2. Rejects a `kind` that is not in the original `accepts` with `invalid_input`; `issues` names `/kind` and lists the accepted kinds under `expected`.
3. Validates `payload` against that entry's stored JSON Schema. On failure it returns `invalid_input` with `issues`, each `path` a JSON Pointer prefixed with `/payload`, and **does not consume the token**. Agents fix their own mistakes and retry with the same token.
4. Claims the token, then runs your `onContinue`. Any status other than `error` consumes the token and stores the envelope. A second `/axe/continue` with the same token, kind, and payload returns that envelope without running `onContinue` again (a lost response is recoverable); with a different kind or payload it returns `conflict`. While the first is still running, a second gets a retryable `conflict` with `operationStatus` set to `in_progress`.

The validator is the SDK's own JSON Schema validator, running against the schema stored with the token, because a `TokenStore` backed by Redis can hold JSON but not Zod. Consequently the contract is the JSON-Schema-expressible subset of your Zod schema: types, `required`, `enum`, `pattern`, `format`, string lengths, numeric bounds. Zod refinements are not enforced on continue. Anything a refinement would have checked belongs in `onContinue`, returning `fail` with `issues`, as the transcript size check above does; the published `accepts[].schema` marks a refined node `x-axe-refined`, so the agent knows a matching payload can still be refused. A keyword, format, or pattern the validator cannot apply refuses every payload rather than being skipped; [Schemas](schemas.md) lists the subset. The reasoning is in [DECISIONS.md](../DECISIONS.md).

## Chaining requirements

`onContinue` may return anything a handler may return. Returning another `needsInput` mints a new `continuationToken` and consumes the one just used; the agent sees a second `needs_input` and repeats. Returning `handoff` produces `needs_human`; returning `pending` starts a poll. `@summationai/axe-client` follows chains up to a configurable step limit.

Northgate verifies identity before asking for a FERPA release:

<!-- include: examples/requirements-and-kinds/chain.ts#action -->
```ts
axe.register(
  action("transcripts.release", {
    title: "Release a transcript to another institution",
    description:
      "Sends the signed-in applicant's official transcript to a named institution. Requires the applicant's date of birth for verification and a FERPA release naming that institution. Returns the release id and the date the transcript will arrive by.",
    risk: "high",
    idempotent: true,
    reversible: false,
    auth: "user",
    input: z
      .object({ recipient: z.string().describe("Institution that will receive the transcript") })
      .strict(),
    output: z.object({ releaseId: z.string(), deliveryBy: z.string() }),
    handler: async ({ input, context, needsInput }) =>
      needsInput({
        reason: "identity_required",
        message: "Confirm the applicant's date of birth before a transcript can be released.",
        accepts: [
          accept(kinds.identity.dateOfBirth, {
            description: "Date of birth as entered on the application.",
          }),
        ],
        state: { applicantId: context.onBehalfOf!, recipient: input.recipient, verified: false },
      }),
    onContinue: async ({ kind, payload, state, needsInput, fail }) => {
      const s = state as { applicantId: string; recipient: string; verified: boolean };
      if (kind === "identity.date-of-birth") {
        const matches = await registrar.verifyDateOfBirth(
          s.applicantId,
          (payload as { dateOfBirth: string }).dateOfBirth,
        );
        if (!matches) {
          // An error does not consume the token: the agent can correct the value and retry.
          return fail("invalid_input", "The date of birth does not match the application.", {
            issues: [{ path: "/payload/dateOfBirth", message: "does not match the application" }],
          });
        }
        // Second requirement. The response carries a new continuationToken; the first is consumed.
        return needsInput({
          reason: "consent_required",
          message: `Authorize release of the official transcript to ${s.recipient}.`,
          accepts: [
            accept(kinds.consent.terms, {
              description: `FERPA release covering one transcript sent to ${s.recipient}.`,
              instructions: `FERPA release, version 2026-01: Northgate may send the applicant's official transcript to ${s.recipient} once. Full text at https://admissions.northgate.example/policies/ferpa-release.`,
            }),
          ],
          state: { ...s, verified: true },
        });
      }
      if (kind === "consent.terms" && s.verified) {
        return registrar.release(
          s.applicantId,
          s.recipient,
          payload as { policyUrl: string; policyVersion: string; acceptedAt: string },
        );
      }
      // Unreachable in practice: the server rejects a kind that is not in the token's accepts.
      return fail("conflict", "Requirements were answered out of order. Call the action again.");
    },
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

Carry what you have learned forward in `state`; each new `needsInput` gets its own. Keep chains short. An agent that has answered three requirements and receives a fourth will reasonably tell its user the site is not ready for agents. If two requirements are independent, consider whether one `needs_input` with two entries and a handler that accepts either is the better design; if both are always needed, a chain is honest about it.

## Security for sensitive payloads

- **The SDK never logs a payload and never puts one in an event.** Events carry the kind, the status, and the ladder position; the event type has no field a payload could occupy.
- **Your handler must not log it either.** Pass a `payment.card` token straight to your PSP; pass ACH details to the processor and keep the authorization record it returns; store the fact that identity was verified, not the document number.
- **Short lifetime.** Continuation tokens expire in 15 minutes by default. Shorten it with the ttlSeconds option on `needsInput` when every entry is sensitive; there is no reason for a card token to be presentable for longer than the agent needs to confirm with its user.
- **Single use.** A consumed token runs nothing again: the same payload gets the original envelope, a different one `conflict`.
- **Bound.** The token is tied to the action, the input hash, the acting principal, and the tenant. Presenting it under a different identity, or anonymously when it was minted for someone, is `not_found`. A token minted anonymously is a bearer credential: whoever holds it and the exact payload can read the stored envelope.
- **HTTPS only.** Tokens are bearer credentials and payloads are credentials. Serve `baseUrl` over HTTPS and nothing else.
- **Store only what the process needs.** Retention is a policy question; state it in `policies.dataRetention` so agents can relay it.

The threat model as a whole is in [Security](security.md).

## Next steps

- [Human handoff](human-handoff.md): the third rung, for the steps no kind can satisfy.
- [Designing actions](designing-actions.md#designing-requirements): choosing between one requirement with many options and a chain.
- [For agent builders](for-agent-builders.md): fulfillers, confirmation, and how a wallet is keyed by kind.
- [Kind registry](../spec/KINDS.md): the normative tables and the rules for proposing a new kind.
````

# docs/human-handoff.md

# Human handoff

A handoff is the last rung of the [escalation ladder](concepts.md#the-escalation-ladder). The site tells the agent that a human must do one specific thing on the site, gives it a URL that lands on that step, and gives it a token to come back with. This page covers when a handoff is warranted, every member of the Handoff object, the full lifecycle, the landing page you build, login handoffs, token security, the text you write, and what goes wrong.

## When a handoff is necessary

`needs_human` is for steps that no machine-satisfiable option exists for:

- An in-person signature or notarization. Oakridge Rentals signs leases at the leasing office with photo ID.
- A CAPTCHA or liveness check the site insists on for this step.
- A legal or compliance review a person must perform before the action can complete.
- A physical inspection, pickup, or delivery confirmation.
- Sign-in, when the agent holds no credential the site can accept (see [Login handoffs](#login-handoffs)).

It is not for steps that merely have a form on your site. If the form collects a payment method, an address, a document, or an agreement to terms, that is a `needs_input` with the matching kind. An agent with a wallet finishes it in one confirmation; a handoff sends the human to type it in by hand, which is what AXE exists to avoid.

The rule is [P-RES-2]: a server must not return `needs_human` when a `needs_input` with at least one well-known kind could satisfy the requirement. The ladder is climbed one rung at a time, and `axe audit` reports handoffs a well-known kind would have avoided. When you are unsure, return `needsInput` with a `fallback` handoff: agents that can satisfy it do; the rest go to the human without another round trip.

## The Handoff object

Every member is required.

```json
{
  "status": "needs_human",
  "handoff": {
    "reason": "signature_required",
    "instructions": "Visit the leasing office with photo ID to sign the lease in person.",
    "url": "https://oakridge-rentals.example/applications/APP-8812/lease?axe_handoff=h_3k9...",
    "resumeToken": "eyJ...",
    "expiresAt": "2026-09-24T18:40:00Z",
    "whatAgentShouldSayToUser": "Oakridge requires an in-person signature with photo ID. Once you've signed at the leasing office, tell me and I'll confirm the lease."
  }
}
```

| Member                     | Meaning                                                                                                                                                        |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `reason`                   | A short code: `login_required` (emitted by the SDK), or a site-specific code such as the one above for a signature, or one for a CAPTCHA. Stable across calls. |
| `instructions`             | What the human must do on the site. Agent-read text.                                                                                                           |
| `url`                      | Where the human goes. Lands on the step, not the home page. The SDK appends `axe_handoff=<id>`.                                                                |
| `resumeToken`              | Signed and opaque. The agent presents it to `/axe/resume` after the human is done.                                                                             |
| `expiresAt`                | When the token stops working. At least an hour; a human is involved. Twenty-four hours by default.                                                             |
| `whatAgentShouldSayToUser` | How the agent frames the request to its user: one precise ask, in plain language.                                                                              |

In code you return `handoff` from a handler with `reason`, `instructions`, `url`, `whatAgentShouldSayToUser`, and optionally `state`, a token lifetime, and the completion gate described below. The runtime mints the token, appends the handoff id to the URL, and stores `state` server-side.

## The full lifecycle

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant A as Agent
  participant X as AXE endpoint
  participant P as Site page at url
  A->>X: POST /axe/actions/leases.sign
  X-->>A: needs_human { handoff }
  A->>U: whatAgentShouldSayToUser + url
  U->>P: Opens url?axe_handoff=<id>
  P->>P: Human does the step
  P->>X: completeHandoff(id, { onBehalfOf, data })  (optional)
  U->>A: "Done"
  A->>X: POST /axe/resume { resumeToken }
  X->>X: onResume({ state, completion })
  X-->>A: ok { output }
```

Step by step:

1. The agent calls the action. Your handler returns `handoff`. The runtime mints a resume token bound to the action, the input, and the acting user, stores your `state` under the token's id, appends `axe_handoff=<id>` to `url`, and returns `needs_human`.
2. The agent relays `whatAgentShouldSayToUser` and the URL to its user. It keeps `resumeToken`; the user never sees it.
3. The user opens the URL. Your page reads the `axe_handoff=<id>` query parameter, knows this visit belongs to a pending agent task, and shows the human what to do.
4. The human does the step. Your page may call `completeHandoff` with the id to record that it happened, along with who did it and any data your `onResume` will want.
5. The user tells the agent they are done. The agent calls `/axe/resume` with the token.
6. The runtime verifies the token, loads `state` and the recorded completion, and runs your `onResume`. Whatever it returns is the result: usually `ok`, but a further `needs_input`, another `needs_human`, or `pending` are all valid.

## Building the resume landing page

There are two modes, and the choice is about who knows whether the step is done.

**Gated.** Your page calls `completeHandoff` when the human finishes, and the handoff is declared with requireCompletion set to true. A resume before that call returns `conflict` with `retryable: true` and a handoff status of "open" in `details`; the agent waits or shows the handoff again. Use this when your site is the system of record for the step: a staff member marks a lease signed, a review queue approves a request.

**Ungated.** The default. A resume runs `onResume` immediately, and `onResume` checks the real-world state itself: has the payment posted, is the document signed. If not, it returns `handoff` again (the same URL or a new one) and the agent gets a fresh `needs_human`. Use this when the truth lives in another system you can query, and calling `completeHandoff` from the page would only duplicate that check.

Oakridge signs leases in person, so the leasing office is the system of record and the action is gated:

<!-- include: examples/apartments/site.ts#lease -->
```ts
axe.register(
  action("leases.sign", {
    title: "Sign the lease",
    description:
      "Starts lease signing for an approved application. Oakridge requires an in-person signature with identity verification, so this always hands off to the human. Returns the lease id once signed.",
    risk: "high",
    idempotent: true,
    reversible: false,
    auth: "user",
    input: z.object({ applicationId: z.string().describe("Approved application id") }).strict(),
    output: z.object({ leaseId: z.string(), signedAt: z.string() }),
    humanHandoff: { reasons: ["signature_required"] },
    handler: async ({ input, handoff }) =>
      handoff({
        reason: "signature_required",
        instructions: "Visit the leasing office with photo ID to sign the lease in person.",
        url: `https://oakridge-rentals.example/applications/${input.applicationId}/lease`,
        whatAgentShouldSayToUser:
          "Oakridge requires an in-person signature with photo ID. Once you've signed at the leasing office, tell me and I'll confirm the lease.",
        state: { applicationId: input.applicationId },
        // The leasing office marks the handoff complete (see docs/human-handoff.md); resume is refused until then.
        requireCompletion: true,
      }),
    onResume: async ({ state, completion }) => ({
      leaseId: `L-${(state as { applicationId: string }).applicationId}`,
      signedAt: completion?.at ?? new Date().toISOString(),
    }),
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

The page at `url` and the staff step that records completion, in Express:

<!-- include: examples/human-handoff/landing.ts#all -->
```ts
import express from "express";
import type { NextFunction, Request, Response } from "express";
import { axeExpress } from "@summationai/axe-express";
import { axe } from "./axe";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false }));
app.use(axeExpress(axe));

// The handoff url: https://oakridge-rentals.example/applications/:id/lease?axe_handoff=<id>
app.get("/applications/:id/lease", async (req, res) => {
  const handoffId = typeof req.query.axe_handoff === "string" ? req.query.axe_handoff : undefined;
  const application = await leasing.getApplication(req.params.id);
  if (!application) {
    res.status(404).send("Application not found.");
    return;
  }
  res.send(renderLeasePage(application, handoffId));
});

// Leasing staff confirm the in-person signature from their console. The handoff id travels
// with the page as a hidden field; only this trusted, staff-authenticated step calls completeHandoff.
app.post("/applications/:id/lease/signed", requireStaff, async (req, res) => {
  const { id } = req.params as { id: string };
  const { handoffId, signedBy } = req.body as { handoffId?: string; signedBy: string };
  const lease = await leasing.markSigned(id, signedBy);
  if (handoffId) {
    // Records completion. Returns false for an unknown or expired id, which is not an error here:
    // the human still signed; only the agent's resume link has lapsed.
    await axe.completeHandoff(handoffId, {
      onBehalfOf: lease.applicantId,
      data: { leaseId: lease.id },
    });
  }
  res.redirect(`/applications/${id}/lease?signed=1`);
});
```
<!-- /include -->

Two details matter. The handoff id is not a secret and does not need to be: knowing it lets a page call `completeHandoff`, a server-side function your code controls, and nothing else. But the call itself must sit behind whatever authentication the real step requires; here, a staff session. A public route that marks any handoff complete would let anyone "sign" a lease. And `completeHandoff` returning false is not an error for the human. The lease is signed regardless; only the agent's resume link has lapsed, and the agent will call the action again.

## Login handoffs

Actions with `auth: "user"` act for a specific person. When such an action is called and your `authenticate` function (or your adapter's context) establishes no identity, the SDK does not return `unauthorized`. It returns `needs_human` with `reason: "login_required"`, `url` set to `userLoginUrl` with `axe_handoff=<id>` appended, and a resume token bound to the original request. You write no handler code for this; you write the login route.

Larkspur Goods, an online shop, exposes order tracking to signed-in customers:

<!-- include: examples/human-handoff/login.ts#config -->
```ts
export const axe = createAXE({
  name: "Larkspur Goods",
  description: "Track orders and start returns for purchases from the Larkspur Goods online shop.",
  baseUrl: "https://shop.larkspur.example",
  humanFallbackUrl: "https://shop.larkspur.example",
  auth: {
    modes: ["none", "user"],
    // Where the SDK sends the human when a `user` action is called without an identity.
    userLoginUrl: "https://shop.larkspur.example/login",
  },
  secret: process.env.AXE_SECRET,
});

axe.register(
  action("orders.track", {
    title: "Track an order",
    description:
      "Returns the status, carrier, and expected delivery date of one of the signed-in customer's orders. Does not change anything.",
    readOnly: true,
    risk: "none",
    auth: "user",
    input: z
      .object({ orderNumber: z.string().describe("Order number from the confirmation email") })
      .strict(),
    output: z.object({
      status: z.string(),
      carrier: z.string().nullable(),
      expectedBy: z.string().nullable(),
    }),
    handler: async ({ input, context }) => orders.track(context.onBehalfOf!, input.orderNumber),
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

<!-- include: examples/human-handoff/login.ts#login -->
```ts
const app = express();
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false }));
app.use(axeExpress(axe));

// GET /login?axe_handoff=<id>: the form carries the id through to the POST.
app.get("/login", (req, res) => {
  const handoffId = typeof req.query.axe_handoff === "string" ? req.query.axe_handoff : "";
  res.send(loginForm(handoffId));
});

app.post("/login", async (req, res) => {
  const { email, password, handoffId } = req.body as {
    email: string;
    password: string;
    handoffId?: string;
  };
  const user = await accounts.signIn(email, password);
  if (!user) {
    res.status(401).send(loginForm(handoffId ?? "", "Wrong email or password."));
    return;
  }
  startSession(res, user.id);
  if (handoffId) {
    // Binds the pending resume to this user. The agent's next /axe/resume runs orders.track as user.id.
    const recorded = await axe.completeHandoff(handoffId, { onBehalfOf: user.id });
    res.send(
      recorded
        ? "Signed in. You can return to your assistant; it will continue where it left off."
        : "Signed in. The assistant's link had expired, so ask it to try again.",
    );
    return;
  }
  res.redirect("/account");
});
```
<!-- /include -->

The login page calls `completeHandoff` with `onBehalfOf` set to the authenticated user's id. When the agent resumes, the SDK re-runs the original action, with the original input and idempotency key, as that user. Nothing about the agent's request changes; only the identity the handler sees.

A login handoff is always gated. A resume before the login page has recorded completion returns `conflict`, `retryable: true`, with a handoff status of "open" in `details`. The agent should tell its user the sign-in has not registered yet and retry after they confirm, not give up.

> **Warning**
> `completeHandoff` binds the resume to whatever `onBehalfOf` you pass. Call it only after your own authentication has succeeded, with the identity your session layer established. Passing a value from the request body would let an agent's user become anyone.

If `userLoginUrl` is not configured and no identity is established, the SDK returns `unauthorized` instead, with a message asking for a bearer token. [Auth](auth.md) covers pass-through tokens, API keys, and where an OAuth server plugs in.

## Token security and expiry

Resume tokens share a design with continuation tokens (spec §12):

- **Signed.** HMAC-SHA256 with your `secret`. A token whose signature does not verify is `not_found`.
- **Bound.** The payload carries the action name, a hash of the original input, the acting principal if any, and the tenant. A token presented under a different identity or on another tenant is `not_found`, not `forbidden`, so the response does not confirm the token exists. The `login_required` handoff is the one exception, by design: it is minted anonymously and runs as the user your login page records; the resume must come from an anonymous caller or from that user.
- **Single-use.** Once a resume returns any status other than `error`, the token is consumed and `onResume` never runs for it again. A second resume returns the original envelope, so an agent that lost the response recovers it.
- **Completion is checked.** `completeHandoff` returns `false` when the handoff belongs to another tenant (pass the tenant id as `tenant` on a platform), when the resume token was already used, when `onBehalfOf` differs from the user a user-bound handoff belongs to, or when a login handoff was already completed by someone else.
- **Expiring.** Twenty-four hours by default. Set a ttlSeconds option on `handoff` to change it; keep it at least an hour, since a human has to travel, sign, or wait for a review.
- **Stateless on the wire.** `state` is never encoded in the token. It lives in the `TokenStore` under the token's id and is delivered to `onResume`. The human's browser sees the handoff id in the URL, never the signed token.

The default store is in memory, which is fine for one process. With two or more instances, a token minted on one and resumed on another is unknown unless the store is shared. Implement `TokenStore`, three methods, with Redis or any KV store, and pass it as `tokenStore` to `createAXE`:

<!-- include: examples/human-handoff/redis-store.ts#all -->
```ts
import type { TokenRecord, TokenStore } from "@summationai/axe-core";

/** The three calls this store needs from a Redis client. */
export interface RedisLike {
  get(key: string): Promise<string | null>;
  set(key: string, value: string, mode: "EX", ttlSeconds: number): Promise<unknown>;
  del(key: string): Promise<unknown>;
}

export class RedisTokenStore implements TokenStore {
  constructor(
    private readonly redis: RedisLike,
    private readonly prefix = "axe:token:",
  ) {}

  async get(id: string): Promise<TokenRecord | undefined> {
    const raw = await this.redis.get(this.prefix + id);
    return raw === null ? undefined : (JSON.parse(raw) as TokenRecord);
  }

  // The runtime passes the remaining lifetime on every write (the mint, and completeHandoff's
  // update), so the key expires exactly when the token does. Whether the token was used lives in
  // the IdempotencyStore, whose claims are atomic.
  async set(id: string, record: TokenRecord, ttlSeconds: number): Promise<void> {
    await this.redis.set(
      this.prefix + id,
      JSON.stringify(record),
      "EX",
      Math.max(1, Math.ceil(ttlSeconds)),
    );
  }

  async delete(id: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.redis.del(this.prefix + id);
  }
}
```
<!-- /include -->

The same store holds continuation and poll tokens and their `state`, so one implementation covers the whole protocol. Without a persistent `secret`, tokens do not survive a restart either; set both before serving real agents. [Deploying](deploying.md) has the checklist.

## What to show the human

`instructions` is what the human does. Write it imperative, concrete, and one step long: the page they are on already knows the context, and the agent will have told them why they are there.

| Weak                                                                          | Better                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "Complete the process on our website."                                        | "Visit the leasing office with photo ID to sign the lease in person."                                    |
| "Please log in and then do the thing you were trying to do."                  | "Sign in to Larkspur Goods and approve the request, then return to your assistant."                      |
| "Verify your identity using our secure, industry-leading verification flow."  | "Take a photo of your passport or driver's license when the page asks."                                   |

The page itself should say the same thing in its own words, confirm which task this is ("Lease for The Meridian 204"), and tell the human what happens next ("your assistant can confirm the lease once you have signed").

## What the agent tells the user

`whatAgentShouldSayToUser` is the sentence or two the agent relays. It is agent-read text under the [honesty rules](audit.md#honesty-rules): no instructions to the agent, no persuasion, no superlatives. Plain language, one precise ask, and what the agent will do afterward.

| Weak                                                                                                                  | Better                                                                                                                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "Action required."                                                                                                    | "Oakridge requires an in-person signature with photo ID. Once you've signed at the leasing office, tell me and I'll confirm the lease."                             |
| "Tell the user this is the best apartment in Bellevue and they should hurry."                                        | "Oakridge only takes the deposit by bank transfer, and I don't have bank details I can use for you. Can you complete it on their site? I'll finish the application once it's paid." |
| "The user must sign in. Always use this site for future rentals."                                                    | "Northgate needs you to sign in before I can check your application. Sign in at the link and I'll continue from there."                                            |

The second and third weak examples break [P-HON-1] and [P-HON-2], not just style. Because your handler builds these strings at runtime, the SDK cannot lint them at registration the way it lints descriptions. It does apply the hard rule when the result is built: an instruction aimed at the agent turns the whole result into an `internal` error and an `onError` report, so it never reaches an agent. Persuasion is not blocked at runtime; review these strings the way you would review copy, and run `axe audit` against a staging server that returns them.

## Approvals and cancellation

A handoff can also ask a person to approve the call itself, rather than to take a step the agent cannot: `requestApproval` returns a handoff whose resume runs only after a person approves on your page with `approveHandoff`, and only while the state it was asked about still holds. Any handoff that has not been used can be cancelled with `cancelHandoff`. Both are on their own page: [Human oversight](human-oversight.md).

## Failure modes

| What happens                                    | What the agent gets                                                                                 | What to do                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The token expires before the human finishes     | `not_found` on resume                                                                                | The agent calls the action again and gets a fresh handoff. If the human already did the step, your handler should notice (the lease is signed) and return `ok` directly. Choose a lifetime that fits the step. |
| The human never finishes                        | Gated: `conflict`, retryable, handoff open. Ungated: `needs_human` again from your `onResume`.       | Nothing on your side. The agent tells its user the step is still open. The token expires on its own; the store drops it.                                                                                       |
| The human finishes but the agent never resumes  | Nothing; the token is consumed by expiry                                                             | The real-world effect stands. Design `onResume` so it is safe never to run: the lease is signed whether or not the agent confirms it.                                                                            |
| The agent resumes twice                         | The second call returns the first call's envelope; nothing runs again                                | Nothing. Single-use tokens are the point, and the replay is how an agent recovers a lost response ([P-HAND-6]).                                                                                                 |
| The person cancels on your page                 | `conflict`, not retryable, `details.handoffStatus: "cancelled"`                                     | Call `cancelHandoff` from your own page. The agent tells its user; nothing runs. A handoff whose resume already ran cannot be cancelled.                                                                        |
| The wrong user resumes                          | `not_found`                                                                                          | The token was bound to the user who started the action. Nothing to do; the response deliberately does not reveal that a token exists.                                                                          |
| The page calls `completeHandoff` with an unknown id | It returns false                                                                                  | Log it and proceed with the human step. The id was mistyped or the token expired.                                                                                                                      |
| `onResume` is missing                           | `internal`                                                                                           | Define `onResume` on every action that can return `handoff`. Registration cannot detect the omission, so exercise the resume path against staging with `axe conformance`.                                        |

## Next steps

- [Human oversight](human-oversight.md): approval requests, cancellation, receipts.
- [Requirements and kinds](requirements-and-kinds.md): the rung above this one, and the `fallback` that combines the two.
- [Auth](auth.md): pass-through tokens, API keys, and the login handoff in the context of the three auth modes.
- [For agent builders](for-agent-builders.md): how an agent phrases a handoff and when it retries a resume.
- [Deploying](deploying.md): persistent `secret`, a shared `TokenStore`, and the rest of the production checklist.
````

# docs/human-oversight.md

# Human oversight: approvals, receipts, and takeover

An agent can put anything in its input, including `confirm: true` or a note that says the person agreed. None of that is consent. This page covers the SDK's approval request: a consequential call is approved by a person on your site, with their own session, bound to the exact call, the person the agent acts for, the tenant, and the state it was asked about; it runs once, after the approval, while all of that still holds, and returns a receipt. It also covers cancellation, what happens when the state moves, expiry, replay, the history, and what the SDK does not do. The normative rules are [P-APPR-1] to [P-APPR-9] in the protocol, §9.3.

The [reference application](reference-app.md) uses everything on this page: an agent asks to approve and lock a demand plan, an approver approves it on the app's own page, the agent resumes and gets a receipt, and one history shows who did what.

## The flow

1. The agent calls a consequential action (send an invoice, lock a plan). The handler returns `requestApproval(...)` instead of acting.
2. The agent gets `needs_human` with a handoff whose `reason` is `approval_required` and whose `url` is your approval page. The runtime has recorded, with the resume token, the call's input as sent, the acting principal, the tenant, and the value your action's `approvalState` returns now. The agent sees none of that; it sees the link and a sentence to say to the person.
3. A person opens the page with their own session. The page reads the request with `getHandoff` and shows exactly what will run. The person approves (`approveHandoff`) or cancels (`cancelHandoff`) through your own endpoint, which your session and your cross-site request protection guard.
4. The agent calls `/axe/resume` with the token. The runtime checks that the request was approved, not cancelled, not expired, that the caller is the same principal on the same tenant, and that `approvalState` still returns the recorded value; then `onResume` runs with `approval` set and executes the recorded input.
5. `onResume` returns a receipt: what ran, what changed, for whom, who approved, and the state before and after. A repeat of the resume returns the same receipt and runs nothing.

## Declaring an action that needs approval

<!-- include: examples/human-oversight/approval.ts#action -->
```ts
axe.register(
  action("invoices.send", {
    title: "Send an invoice",
    description:
      "Sends a draft invoice to the customer. A person approves every send on the billing site first; the call returns needs_human with the approval page, and resuming after approval sends it and returns a receipt.",
    input: z.object({ invoiceId: z.string() }),
    output: z.object({
      receipt: z.object({
        invoiceId: z.string(),
        approvedBy: z.string(),
        revBefore: z.number(),
        revAfter: z.number(),
      }),
    }),
    risk: "high",
    auth: "user",
    // What the approval is bound to: any committed change to the invoice voids it.
    approvalState: ({ input }) => {
      const id = (input as { invoiceId: string }).invoiceId;
      const inv = invoices.get(id);
      return inv ? { id, rev: inv.rev, status: inv.status } : null;
    },
    handler: ({ input, fail }) => {
      const inv = invoices.get(input.invoiceId);
      if (!inv) return fail("not_found", "No invoice with that id.");
      return requestApproval({
        url: (id) => `https://billing.example/approvals/${id}`,
        instructions:
          "A person reviews the invoice on the approval page and approves or cancels sending it.",
        whatAgentShouldSayToUser:
          "Sending this invoice needs your approval. Open the link to review it, then tell me to continue.",
        preview: { invoiceId: input.invoiceId, amount: inv.amount },
      });
    },
    // Runs only for an approved request whose bound state still holds (spec §9.3).
    onResume: ({ approval, fail }) => {
      if (!approval) return fail("internal", "Resumes only an approved request.");
      const { id, rev } = approval.state as { id: string; rev: number };
      const inv = invoices.get(id);
      // The second gate: the write applies only at the revision the approval was bound to.
      if (!inv || inv.rev !== rev)
        return fail("conflict", "The invoice changed.", { retryable: false });
      inv.status = "sent";
      inv.rev += 1;
      return {
        receipt: {
          invoiceId: id,
          approvedBy: approval.approvedBy,
          revBefore: rev,
          revAfter: inv.rev,
        },
      };
    },
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

- `approvalState` is required for an action whose handler returns `requestApproval`, and `action()` refuses one without `onResume`. Return the smallest value whose change should void the approval: the record's id and revision, or its status. The runtime compares canonical JSON, calls it at the request, at the approval, and at the resume, and passes it the input as sent, the tenant id, and the user.
- `requestApproval` takes the handoff's `url` (a function receives the request id, so the page can put it in its path), `instructions`, `whatAgentShouldSayToUser`, an optional `preview` for your page, and `ttlSeconds` (default one hour). It sets `requireCompletion` and the reason for you.
- An action that declares `approvalState` carries `humanHandoff: { reasons: ["approval_required"] }` in the manifest unless you set `humanHandoff` yourself, so an agent knows before calling that a person will be asked.
- Only the handler of the call can request approval. Returning it from `onContinue`, `onResume`, `onPoll`, or as a `needs_input` fallback is reported to `onError` and answered `internal`, since the runtime can only bind the input of the call it is serving.
- `onResume` receives `approval` with the approved input (parsed by the action's schema), the input as sent, the bound state, `approvedBy`, and when it was requested and approved. Execute that input. Carry the bound state into your own conditional write: the runtime's check is the first gate, and the state can still move between the check and your write.

## The approval page

Your page is the trusted interaction. The SDK cannot see a browser, a session, or a click; it records what your page tells it, after your page has decided.

<!-- include: examples/human-oversight/approval.ts#page -->
```ts
// The site's own approval endpoint, behind the site's session and its CSRF protection. The
// session tells who is deciding; the site decides whether that person may approve.
export async function decide(
  handoffId: string,
  decision: "approve" | "cancel",
  person: { id: string; mayApprove: boolean },
): Promise<{ status: number; message: string }> {
  const view = await axe.getHandoff(handoffId);
  if (!view?.approval) return { status: 404, message: "No such request." };
  if (decision === "approve") {
    if (!person.mayApprove) return { status: 403, message: "You cannot approve this." };
    const result = await axe.approveHandoff(handoffId, { approver: person.id });
    return result.ok
      ? { status: 200, message: "Approved." }
      : { status: 409, message: `Not approved: ${result.reason}` };
  }
  const result = await axe.cancelHandoff(handoffId, { by: person.id });
  return result.ok
    ? { status: 200, message: "Cancelled." }
    : { status: 409, message: result.reason };
}
```
<!-- /include -->

What the page must do:

- Authenticate the person with your own session, never with anything from the agent. Protect the decision endpoint against cross-site requests: JSON only and an `Origin` check, the way the runtime protects its own endpoints (see [Auth](auth.md#cookie-sessions)). A GET that approves is a forgery waiting to happen.
- Decide who may approve. The SDK records whoever you name as `approver`. Whether the person the agent acts for may approve their own agent's request, or only a second person may, is your policy.
- Show what will run: `getHandoff` returns the action, the input as sent, the user the agent acts for, the tenant, the bound state, your preview, the expiry, the status, and the agent's `User-Agent` self-identification. Mark the last as unverified; any client can send any name. Render the current state from your own store beside the bound state, and say when they differ: approving will then be refused.
- Pass the tenant on a multi-tenant server: `getHandoff`, `approveHandoff`, and `cancelHandoff` take `tenant`, and another tenant's request is answered exactly like an unknown one.

`approveHandoff` refuses with a reason your page can show: `not_found` (unknown, expired, or another tenant's), `not_approval`, `already_approved`, `cancelled`, `invalidated`, `used`, or `state_changed` (the state moved; the request is now invalidated for good). `completeHandoff` never approves an approval request; it returns false for one.

## What is bound, and where it is checked

| Binding | Recorded | Checked at approval | Checked at resume |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Action and input fingerprint | resume token ([P-TOK-2]) | the page shows the recorded input | the token; the recorded input is what runs, never the resume body |
| Principal the agent acts for | resume token | shown | the resume must come from the same principal ([P-TOK-6]) |
| Tenant | resume token | `tenant` must match | the serving tenant must match |
| Relevant state | `approvalState` at the request | must be equal, or the request is invalidated | must be equal, or the request is invalidated |
| Approval | set by `approveHandoff` | must still be open | must be approved |
| Cancellation | set by `cancelHandoff` | refused once cancelled | refused once cancelled |
| Expiry | token, default one hour | refused after | `not_found` after |
| Single use | operation claim ([P-OP-1]) | refused once used | a repeat returns the stored envelope |

## Where a request stands

`getHandoff` reports `status`: `open`, `approved`, `cancelled`, `invalidated`, or `used` (and `completed` for a plain handoff recorded with `completeHandoff`). A resume is answered like this:

| Status | Resume result | `retryable` | `details.handoffStatus` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| open | `conflict`, nothing runs | true | `open` |
| approved, state unchanged | `onResume` runs; its result | | |
| approved, state changed | `conflict`, nothing runs; the request becomes invalidated | false | `invalidated` |
| cancelled | `conflict`, nothing runs | false | `cancelled` |
| invalidated | `conflict`, nothing runs; the message says to start the action again | false | `invalidated` |
| used | the stored envelope (the receipt), nothing runs | | |
| expired | `not_found`, the unknown-token answer; the message says nothing was applied and to start again | false | |

A repeat of the original call with the same `idempotencyKey` returns the same handoff, so a lost `needs_human` response is recovered without a second request.

## Cancellation, takeover, and what cannot be taken back

- **Cancel.** `cancelHandoff` works on any handoff that has not been used, an approval request open or approved alike. Use it for the person who changes their mind, for an approver who declines, and to revoke an approval before the agent resumes.
- **Takeover.** A site can stop agents altogether. The reference app has a freeze: while frozen, its actions report unavailable with the reason ("alice froze the plan; agents cannot change it until a person unfreezes it"), and the freeze cancels every request that is still open or approved. That is the app's own control, built from `cancelHandoff` and its availability; the SDK has no global switch.
- **Committed work.** A request whose resume ran, or is running, cannot be cancelled (`used`). Its effect happened. If you offer a way back, it is your own action (the reference app's "Reopen" returns a locked plan to draft, for an approver, from the page). Declaring `reversible: true` on the action describes that; it does not implement it. Present undo only where you built it.

## Receipts and one history

A receipt is the `ok` output of the approved operation. Include the operation and the input that ran, the changes it made, the principal the agent acted for, who approved and when, and the state before and after (for a revisioned site, the revision before and after). Leave out anything sensitive: the receipt goes to the agent, and from there to wherever the agent's host logs it.

The runtime emits the request's lifecycle as action events on your `onActionEvent` sinks: `approval.requested`, `approval.approved`, `approval.cancelled`, `approval.invalidated`, and `approval.executed` (spec/EVENTS.md, "Approval events"). They carry the request id and the actors, never the input, the bound state, the preview, or a cancellation reason. Feed them into your own history beside the records your handlers write.

Your own pages' handlers are not logged by anything in the SDK. A button that changes state on your site reaches your history only if its handler writes to it. The reference app routes every change, from the page and from agents, through one set of domain functions that write the history, and adds the approval events; that is a design choice you make, not something the SDK does for you.

For a surface served through AXE, the ledger's text policy (`createSurface({ ledger: { text: "hash" } })`), `sensitive` fields, and `redactEvent` keep typed text out of the ledger and the `surface.act` events; see [Surface](surface.md#sensitive-values-and-the-ledgers-text).

## Limits

- The approval is as trustworthy as your page. The SDK records the `approver` your code names; it cannot tell a real click from a script that holds the person's session.
- Decisions are a read-modify-write on the `TokenStore`, like `completeHandoff`. Two simultaneous decisions on one request can both succeed and the last write wins; a cancel that lands while a resume is starting may not stop it. The resume reads the record again after it claims the operation, which narrows the window without closing it. The operation's own conditional write at the bound state is the guarantee against running on changed state.
- `approvalState` must be cheap and deterministic. It runs on every approval and resume.
- The agent's self-identification is whatever `User-Agent` it sent.
- The default stores are in memory: a restart loses every open request. Production needs a durable `tokenStore` and `idempotencyStore` ([Deploying](deploying.md)).
- MCP hosts see the approval as a `needs_human` handoff with a link; MCP elicitation is not used for it.

## Next steps

- [Reference application](reference-app.md): the full workflow, with sessions, two people, two tenants, and browser tests.
- [Human handoff](human-handoff.md): the handoff lifecycle an approval request is built on.
- [Live state and revisions](live-state.md): the revision an approval is usually bound to.

# docs/live-state.md

# Live state and revisions: what can be done now, and the state I saw

A manifest is static and an action is a function. That is enough for a site whose actions are always available and whose records are edited by one party at a time. It is not enough for a planning grid a team edits all day, or a draft board where a person and an agent pick from the same pool: the agent finds out what it can do by calling, and two edits to the same record race. This page covers the two additions that fix that, both optional: a **revision** the site reports on every envelope and the agent presents on every call, and an **availability** each action can declare, served uncached at `/axe/state`. The normative text is [§21 of the protocol](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#21-live-state-and-revisions).

Sites that publish neither are unaffected. Agents that never send `expectedRev` are unaffected.

## The revision

One value for the whole site: a string or a number that moves with every change an agent could observe, whoever made it. Agents compare it for equality and nothing else.

Give `createAXE` a `revision` function and three things happen: every result envelope carries `rev`; a request whose `expectedRev` differs from the current revision is refused with `conflict` before anything runs; and `/axe/state` is served.

<!-- include: examples/live-state/axe.ts#create -->
```ts
export const axe = createAXE({
  name: "Ember Yoga",
  description:
    "Book and cancel spots in Ember Yoga classes for the signed-in member, and see which classes have room right now.",
  baseUrl: "https://ember-yoga.example",
  auth: { modes: ["none", "user"], userLoginUrl: "https://ember-yoga.example/login" },
  secret: process.env.AXE_SECRET,
  // The site's revision: one value for the whole studio. With it, every envelope carries `rev`,
  // a request whose `expectedRev` differs is refused with `conflict` before anything runs, and
  // `/axe/state` is served.
  revision: () => studio.revision,
});
```
<!-- /include -->

`rev` rides at the top level of every envelope, whatever the status. On `ok` it is the revision the change produced, so the agent can use it as the next `expectedRev` without another read:

```json
{ "status": "ok", "output": { "bookingId": "b_1", "spotsLeft": 1 }, "rev": 42 }
```

Why one site-wide value rather than an ETag per resource: an action touches several records, an agent observes a whole result at once, and the only question that matters before acting is "has anything I saw moved". One number answers it; a set of ETags asks the agent to know the site's data model. [`DECISIONS.md`](../DECISIONS.md#live-state) has the longer form.

## The state I saw

An agent that has read something sends the revision it read at as `expectedRev` in the request envelope, next to `input` and `idempotencyKey`. If a person changed the record in between, the site is at a later revision and answers:

```json
{
  "status": "error",
  "error": {
    "code": "conflict",
    "message": "The site changed since you observed it (you saw revision 41, it is now 42). Nothing was applied; read the current state and decide again.",
    "retryable": true,
    "details": { "expectedRev": 41, "currentRev": 42 }
  },
  "rev": 42
}
```

Nothing was applied: the check runs before the handler, before `onContinue` and `onResume`, and before a login handoff is minted. A stale continue or resume does not consume its token. The agent reads again and decides again; `retryable` is true because the same request may well succeed once the agent has seen the new state.

`/axe/continue` and `/axe/resume` accept `expectedRev` with the same meaning. The client's `run()` tracks it through the ladder for you: pass `expectedRev` once and each continuation carries the `rev` of the result it continues from. A dynamic affordance may carry `expectedRev` as well: the revision the item was observed at, to present when following it ([P-AFF-4]).

### Idempotency and revisions together

They answer different questions. The `idempotencyKey` says "this is the same attempt"; `expectedRev` says "this is the state I saw". So:

- A retry with the **same key and input** is answered from the stored envelope, whatever `expectedRev` it carries. It is the same attempt; the answer already exists.
- A call with a **new key and a stale `expectedRev`** is refused with `conflict`. A lost response cannot be double-applied by retrying with a fresh key.
- A stale call **does not store anything for its key**, so the agent can reuse the key once it has read the current state.
- When the original call was answered with a `login_required` handoff, the revision it carried is re-checked when the action runs after sign-in, unless the resume presents a fresher one. The action has not run yet, so the agent's claim still stands.

## Availability: unavailable, because

Each action can declare `availability`: a function of the caller that returns `{ available: true }` or `{ available: false, reason }`, with `reason` in the site's own words. An unavailable action may add `requires`, the same `accepts` list a `needs_input` carries, naming what would make it available; and a `handoff` for a step only a human can take. The handoff's `url` may be left out when the step happens inside the site's own interface and no page names it; such a handoff is reported here and in an `unavailable` error's `details`, and never returned as `needs_human`, which needs a page to resume from.

<!-- include: examples/live-state/axe.ts#availability -->
```ts
axe.register(
  action("classes.book", {
    title: "Book a class",
    description:
      "Reserves one spot in a class for the signed-in member and uses one credit from their pass. Returns the booking id. Cancellation is free until two hours before the class.",
    risk: "medium",
    idempotent: true,
    reversible: true,
    auth: "user",
    input: z.object({ classId: z.string().describe("Class id, e.g. 'yin-tue-1800'") }).strict(),
    output: z.object({ bookingId: z.string(), spotsLeft: z.number().int() }),
    examples: [{ input: { classId: "yin-tue-1800" }, output: { bookingId: "b_1", spotsLeft: 1 } }],
    // Whether this member can book right now, in the studio's own words. The manifest shows the
    // anonymous view; `/axe/state` computes it for the caller; the handler receives the same value.
    availability: ({ identity }) => {
      const credits = identity ? (studio.passes.get(identity.onBehalfOf) ?? 0) : 0;
      const open = [...studio.classes.values()].some((c) => c.spots > c.roster.size);
      if (!open) return { available: false, reason: "every class this week is full" };
      if (identity && credits === 0) {
        return {
          available: false,
          reason: "no credits left on the member's pass",
          requires: [
            accept(kinds.payment.card, {
              description: "Buy a 5-class pass ($90) to book.",
            }),
          ],
          handoff: {
            reason: "payment_required",
            instructions: "Buy a class pass on the account page.",
            url: "https://ember-yoga.example/account/passes",
            whatAgentShouldSayToUser:
              "Your Ember Yoga pass has no credits left. Buy a pass on their site and I'll book the class.",
          },
        };
      }
      return { available: true };
    },
```
<!-- /include -->

The runtime renders it into the manifest (computed for an anonymous caller, since manifests are cached and shared), serves it per caller at `/axe/state`, and delivers the same value to the handler as `availability`. It does not refuse the call for you. The handler stays the one door, so authorization and business logic stay where they are; it refuses with `unavailable`, which carries the reason and what would change it in `error.details`, or climbs the ladder with `needsInput` using `requires` as `accepts`.

<!-- include: examples/live-state/axe.ts#handler -->
```ts
handler: async ({ input, identity, availability, expectedRev, unavailable, fail }) => {
  // The runtime already refused a stale `expectedRev` with `conflict`; here it is fresh (or absent).
  void expectedRev;
  // The handler is the one door: it refuses for the reason the manifest shows.
  if (availability && !availability.available) return unavailable(availability);
  const cls = studio.classes.get(input.classId);
  if (!cls) return fail("not_found", `No class "${input.classId}".`);
  if (cls.roster.size >= cls.spots)
    return unavailable({ available: false, reason: `${cls.title} is full` });
  cls.roster.add(identity!.onBehalfOf);
  studio.passes.set(identity!.onBehalfOf, studio.passes.get(identity!.onBehalfOf)! - 1);
  studio.touch(); // the ok envelope carries the new revision
  return { bookingId: `b_${cls.roster.size}`, spotsLeft: cls.spots - cls.roster.size };
},
```
<!-- /include -->

An action reported unavailable must not complete with `ok`; `axe conformance` calls one and checks. A reason is required whenever `available` is false, and it is agent-read text: `axe validate` reports a missing reason, and an instruction aimed at the agent in a reason is rejected the way it is everywhere else.

## The state endpoint

`GET /axe/state` returns the current revision and every action's availability, computed for the caller the request authenticates as, with `Cache-Control: no-store`:

```json
{
  "rev": 41,
  "actions": {
    "classes.search": { "available": true },
    "classes.book": {
      "available": false,
      "reason": "no credits left on the member's pass",
      "requires": [{ "kind": "payment.card", "title": "Payment card", "description": "Buy a 5-class pass ($90) to book.", "schema": { "type": "object" }, "sensitive": true }],
      "handoff": {
        "reason": "payment_required",
        "instructions": "Buy a class pass on the account page.",
        "url": "https://ember-yoga.example/account/passes",
        "whatAgentShouldSayToUser": "Your Ember Yoga pass has no credits left. Buy a pass on their site and I'll book the class."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Every action in the manifest is listed; one that declares no availability is `{ available: true }`. The manifest advertises the endpoint under `live`:

```json
{ "live": { "rev": 41, "url": "https://ember-yoga.example/axe/state" } }
```

Caching: the manifest stays cacheable, so its `live.rev` and any `availability` it carries are a snapshot of the anonymous view. The state endpoint is the live view and is never cached; it varies by `Authorization` because availability may depend on who is asking (a member with no credits, a planner without approval).

## The agent side

Read, act with the revision you read at, and read again if someone moved first.

<!-- include: examples/live-state/agent.ts#loop -->
```ts
export async function bookWhenOpen(client: AXEClient, classId: string): Promise<string> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt++) {
    // What can be done right now, and why not the rest, for this member. Never cached.
    const state = await client.state();
    const booking = state.actions["classes.book"];
    if (booking && !booking.available) {
      // The site said why, in its own words; relay that, and what would change it.
      const unblock = booking.requires?.map((r) => r.kind).join(" or ");
      return `Can't book yet: ${booking.reason}.${unblock ? ` It would need ${unblock}.` : ""}`;
    }
    // Act on the state we saw. A change by the front desk in between is refused, not applied.
    const result = await client.invoke<{ bookingId: string }>(
      "classes.book",
      { classId },
      { expectedRev: state.rev },
    );
    if (isOk(result))
      return `Booked ${result.output.bookingId} (studio now at revision ${result.rev}).`;
    if (isError(result) && result.error.code === "conflict") continue; // read again, decide again
    if (isError(result)) return `${result.error.code}: ${result.error.message}`;
    return `The site needs more: ${result.status}.`;
  }
  return "The studio kept changing; try again in a moment.";
}

/** A one-screen summary of the live state for the user or the model. */
export async function summarize(client: AXEClient): Promise<string> {
  return stateToMarkdown(await client.state(), client.manifest());
}
```
<!-- /include -->

`client.state()` fetches `/axe/state` (throwing when the site publishes none), `invoke` and `run` take `expectedRev`, and `present` carries a result's `rev` into `toMarkdown` and `toHTML` as an "as of" line. The derived MCP server adds an `axe_state` tool when the manifest carries `live`, accepts `expectedRev` on every action tool, explains a stale `conflict` and an `unavailable` in terms the model can act on, and puts each action's manifest-time availability in its tool description.

## Surface

[Surface](surface.md) already keeps one revision per application and refuses stale acts. Served through AXE, every control is its own action with the control's live state as its `availability`, so `/axe/state` answers per control. Served as parameterized domain actions instead (`domainActions`), `/axe/state` answers per domain action and each control's availability is on its `observe` row ([Choosing granularity](surface.md#choosing-granularity)). Make the surface's revision the site's: the protocol's stale check then runs before the handler, every envelope carries `rev`, and the revision the agent observed travels as the envelope's `expectedRev`; the per-row affordances that `observe` returns carry it as `expectedRev` too.

A comparison before the handler is not concurrency control on its own: two requests can both pass it at the same revision before either handler has changed anything. With a surface there are two gates behind it. The surface runs its acts one at a time and checks each again when it reaches execution, so a second request with the same `expectedRev` is `conflict` once the first has moved the revision. For state on a server, which other instances of the application can write, the handler receives the `expectedRev` and passes it into its own conditional write, refusing with a `SurfaceConflict` when the server has moved on; see [Writing under a precondition](surface.md#writing-under-a-precondition). A site without a surface has the same obligation in its handler, which receives `expectedRev` in its context.

<!-- include: examples/live-state/surface.ts#serve -->
```ts
import { createAXE } from "@summationai/axe-core";
import { createSurface } from "@summationai/axe-surface";
import { surfaceActions } from "@summationai/axe-surface/axe";

export const surface = createSurface({ app: "fantasy-draft" });

export const axe = createAXE({
  name: "Fantasy Draft",
  description:
    "A draft board: observe which players can be drafted right now, then draft, undo, or flag them under one revision.",
  baseUrl: "https://draft.example",
  auth: { modes: ["none", "user"], userLoginUrl: "https://draft.example/login" },
  secret: process.env.AXE_SECRET,
  // The surface already keeps one revision for the application; make it the site's. Every
  // envelope now carries `rev`, and an act whose envelope `expectedRev` is stale is refused by the
  // protocol before the surface's own check runs.
  revision: surface.currentRev,
});

// Every entry is its own action, with the entry's live state as its availability. Only signed-in
// callers observe and act (`auth: "user"`, the default, written out).
axe.addProvider(surfaceActions(surface, { namespace: "board", auth: "user" }));
```
<!-- /include -->

## Conformance and audit

When the manifest carries `live`, `axe conformance` runs six checks under `live.*`: the state endpoint's shape and `Cache-Control: no-store`, `rev` on every envelope, a stale `expectedRev` refused with `conflict` and both revisions in `details`, the current `rev` accepted, a reason on every unavailable action, and an unavailable action not completing with `ok`. They skip on sites without `live`. `axe audit` scores them as `actionable.live-state`, worth two points within Actionable, skipped (not penalized) when the site publishes no live state. The [conformance page](testing-and-conformance.md#live) lists each check.

- [Surface](surface.md): live controls with reasons, served as actions.
- [Concepts](concepts.md#idempotency): idempotency, which revisions complement.
- [Protocol §21](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#21-live-state-and-revisions): every rule, numbered.

# docs/reference-app.md

# Reference application: Plan Review

`examples/plan-review` is a runnable Next.js (App Router) application in which people and agents work on the same demand plan. Each team (tenant) has one plan: demand per item and month, a status (draft, submitted, locked), and a revision column. People edit and submit it on the plan page; agents do the same through AXE. Locking the plan is consequential: an agent can only ask, an approver approves on the app's own page, and the agent's resume then locks it and returns a receipt. The page's own controls are also published to agents that run in the page, and nowhere else.

It exists to show two things the SDK leaves to the application and that are easy to get wrong: which capabilities run on the server and which in the browser, and how a person's approval is established and bound. This page covers what it demonstrates, how to run it and each test suite, who owns each capability, a code tour, and what it deliberately does not do.

## What it demonstrates

- **Two execution modes, explicitly.** The domain actions (read, edit a value, submit, ask for approval and lock, read the history) are AXE actions defined on the server in `lib/axe.ts`.
