- **Large outputs are truncated in text.** The JSON block in the text content is cut at 24,000 characters. The structured content always carries the full envelope; hosts that read it lose nothing.
- **No streaming.** A tool call blocks until the result envelope arrives, or until the `pending` poll budget is spent.
- **`axe_poll` takes only URLs the server issued.** The server remembers the `pollUrl` of every `pending` result it returned (the most recent 1000) and refuses any other, so a model cannot make the authenticated client fetch a URL of its choosing. Over HTTP the memory is per session, or per principal in stateless mode, so one session or user cannot poll another's URL ([P-MCP-3](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#22-mcp-mapping)); anonymous stateless callers share one principal. The client's own destination policy (`trust` in the client options) applies on top. A restarted server has forgotten its URLs; the model starts the action again.
- **The poll budget is per server.** The default of 20 seconds is set by the `pollBudgetMs` option of `createMcpServer` and applies to both the initial call and `axe_poll`. `axe_poll` fetches at once, then keeps polling within the budget. Past it, the model must call `axe_poll` again.

- [Auth](auth.md): the three modes and where pass-through tokens come from.

# docs/relay.md

# Relay: an agent in a live tab

A surface lives in the browser tab that created it ([Surface](surface.md), "Where a surface runs"). An agent outside the browser, such as Claude Code, cannot reach it: the controls are closures over that page's state, acting with that page's session. `@summationai/axe-relay` is the SDK's broker for exactly this: the page connects to a relay server, the relay presents the page's surface to agents over MCP, and every act runs in the page, through the page's own `surface.act`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Person] <--> T[Tab: the app's page<br/>surface + connectRelay]
  T <-- WebSocket, relay token --> R[Company-operated MCP service<br/>relay + mirror per tab]
  R <-- MCP: stdio or HTTP + OAuth --> A[Agent]
```

Desktop agents need the service path on this page. The customer application installs only `@summationai/axe-surface` and the browser-only `@summationai/axe-relay/client`; the separately operated service owns the MCP SDK, WebSocket server, agent authentication, and relay records. Browser-native WebMCP remains an additional direct path where the browser supports it.

There are three connection shapes. **Browser handoff** is the recommended provider path: the agent's OAuth identity mints a one-time URL, the client opens the application's ordinary sign-in/page flow, and the installed package connects that attended tab automatically with no pairing code or application backend endpoint. **Development pairing** is the local diagnostic path: the person opens the tab and copies its temporary code. **Unattended host** ([Unattended mode](host.md)) is optional: a host runs a hidden browser session and therefore requires the application to provide a browser-session boundary.

The relay reuses the rest of the SDK: each tab is served through `domainActions` from `@summationai/axe-surface/axe` on a `createAXE` server, and `@summationai/axe-mcp` derives the tools. The revision check, the escalation ladder, the ledger, and the action events are the ones you already have. The normative rules are [S-RELAY-1] to [S-RELAY-14] in [spec/SURFACE.md](../spec/SURFACE.md) §9.1.

## Self-hosted attended mode in four steps

For an application operating its own relay and identity boundary. The provider-operated browser-handoff path below removes steps 2 and 3 from the consuming application's installation.

1. Add the packages: `pnpm add @summationai/axe-surface @summationai/axe-relay`.
2. In the page, register the controls on a surface (or let `@summationai/axe-surface/auto` do it) and connect it:

<!-- include: examples/relay/page.ts#connect -->
```ts
// Your backend mints a short-lived relay token for the signed-in person (see the next example);
// the page asks for one on every connection and before the current one expires.
const relay = connectRelay(surface, {
  url: "wss://relay.yogastudio.example/tab",
  getToken: async () => {
    const res = await fetch("/api/relay-token", { method: "POST", credentials: "same-origin" });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error("not signed in");
    return ((await res.json()) as { token: string }).token;
  },
});
```
<!-- /include -->

3. In your backend, mint the relay token for the signed-in person:

<!-- include: examples/relay/backend.ts#mint -->
```ts
// A signing key used for nothing else, shared with the relay (RELAY_TOKEN_SECRET, at least 32
// characters). The token names the person (sub) and the tenant (org), lives ten minutes, and goes
// to your own page in a response body, never in a URL.
app.post("/api/relay-token", async (req, res) => {
  const user = currentUser(req);
  if (!user) return void res.status(401).json({ error: "sign in" });
  const token = await mintRelayToken(
    { principal: user.id, tenant: user.studioId, ttl: 600, claims: { mid: user.memberId } },
    process.env["RELAY_TOKEN_SECRET"]!,
  );
  res.set("Cache-Control", "no-store").json({ token });
});
```
<!-- /include -->

4. Run the company-side service and connect the agent to it (below: local development now, production with OAuth later).

## Provider browser handoff: no application backend

The Agent Experience service can bind the browser tab directly to the already-authenticated MCP caller. With `RelayOptions.handoff`, an empty `relay_tabs` call returns a short-lived `needs_human` URL. A URL-capable MCP client opens the relay's `/connect/<token>` page; it places a bootstrap in `window.name` and redirects immediately to the configured application URL. After the normal application login completes, `injectedRelay()` recognizes that bootstrap, exchanges it once with `/connect/exchange`, and `connectRelay` attaches the page.

The one-time value is an Agent Experience relay capability, not an application session or API credential. It never appears in the application URL, is exchangeable only from the configured application origin, and is bound to the principal and tenant whose OAuth-authenticated tool call created it. The consuming application installs `@summationai/axe-surface` and `@summationai/axe-relay/client` but adds no token route, session broker, secret, or MCP service. See [`mcp/README.md`](../mcp/README.md#run-the-browser-handoff-service).

## Local development

Start the standalone service under this repository's `mcp/` directory:

```sh
pnpm mcp:dev
```

It serves the website and agent sides separately:

```text
Agent Experience MCP service
  website tabs: ws://127.0.0.1:4717/tab
  desktop agents: http://127.0.0.1:4717/mcp
  service metadata: http://127.0.0.1:4717/.well-known/agent-experience.json
  local bearer key: axd_agent_experience_local
```

In the page, connect with the local-service helper:

<!-- include: examples/relay/page.ts#dev -->
```ts
// Local development against the company-side service (`pnpm mcp:dev` in the SDK checkout): the
// service hands out development tab tokens on loopback and shows an agent pairing code in the tab.
if (location.hostname === "localhost") {
  connectRelay(surface, localMcpService());
}
```
<!-- /include -->

Connect a desktop agent to `http://127.0.0.1:4717/mcp` with the bearer key (see [`mcp/README.md`](../mcp/README.md)). Open the website, then tell the agent the code shown in its Surface indicator. The MCP server instructions tell it to call `relay_tabs`, `relay_pair`, `surface_read`, and `surface_observe`; subsequent Surface tools act on that tab. The indicator changes from the code to "An agent can act in this tab", and to "An agent is acting in this tab" once it has.

The lower-level `axe relay --dev` CLI remains available for SDK development and stdio clients, but application installation instructions point at the standalone service. Only one process can hold port 4717; override the service with `AXE_MCP_PORT` and pass the same service origin to `localMcpService(url)` when needed.

### How a desktop agent discovers the website

An MCP client does not discover this connection from the website URL. Configure the Agent Experience service once in the desktop client at `/mcp`, then start a fresh agent conversation so that client exposes the service's tools and initialization instructions. Those instructions tell the agent to start with `relay_tabs`; the open website announces itself to the service over `/tab`, and `relay_pair` binds the agent to it in local development. After that, `surface_read`, `surface_observe`, `surface_wait`, and the Surface action tools are the website interface.

`/.well-known/agent-experience.json` is non-standard setup metadata for operators and diagnostics. It does not make an MCP client auto-install the service. This boundary is intentional: the browser package knows the tab endpoint, while the desktop client knows the MCP endpoint and agent credential. Neither the consuming website nor its repository hosts an MCP server.

What development mode does, and does not allow:

- `devPairing` listens on loopback only; `--host 0.0.0.0` is refused. Every request must come from a loopback address with a loopback `Host` header, so a web page cannot reach the relay through DNS rebinding.
- Tabs connect from any port on `http://localhost`, `http://127.0.0.1`, or `http://[::1]` (`--origin` replaces the list). Development tokens name the principal `dev` in the tenant `dev`.
- `/mcp` needs `AXE_MCP_AGENT_KEY`. An agent reaches no tab until it pairs with the code shown in one. Five wrong codes lock that agent out for a minute.
- Serve the page over `http://localhost` in development. A page served over `https` that connects to `ws://127.0.0.1` can be blocked as mixed content or stopped by the browser's local network access prompt; use `wss://` for anything that is not local.

## Unattended mode

A host that opens the application in a hidden browser session for a person sets `window.__AXE_RELAY__` with an init script before any page script runs: `{ url, token, mode: "unattended" }`, where `token` is a relay token the host minted for that person. `injectedRelay()` reads it (at call time, never at import, so server rendering is unaffected) and returns `connectRelay` options, or null in a normal browser. `relayOptions(fallback)` returns the injected options when present and your attended options otherwise, so one line covers both:

<!-- include: examples/relay/page.ts#unattended -->
```ts
// One line for both modes: in a hidden session a host opened for the person, the host injected
// the connection (`window.__AXE_RELAY__`: no pairing, no indicator, approvals in the agent's
// client); in a normal browser, the attended development relay below.
export function connectEitherWay(s: Surface): RelayConnection {
  return connectRelay(s, relayOptions(localMcpService()));
}
```
<!-- /include -->

What changes when the tab is unattended:

- No pairing. The host minted the token for the person the session is for, and the agent reaches the tab through its own verified identity (OAuth `identify`, or a stdio relay started for that principal). A development relay still shows pairing codes, which nobody sees in a hidden tab; use a relay with `agentAuth` or `--stdio --principal`.
- No indicator by default (`indicator` is off; the host can pass `indicator: true`). The tab takes approvals from the agent (`approvals: "agent"`), so the relay asks the person in the agent's UI, below.
- Stop from the indicator is absent. The person stops the session by telling the agent (it calls `relay_stop`), from the host's own watch page (the host calls `relay.stop(who)`), or by revoking the agent's OAuth grant, after which the agent reaches no tab at all.

The injected connection replaces the fallback's `url`, token, `mode`, `approvals`, and `indicator`, and keeps its other options (`onStatus`, `requireApproval`, `describe`). A host may also inject `getToken` (an exposed function) for a session that outlives one token.

## What the agent sees

| Tool                  | What it does                                                                                               |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `relay_tabs`          | Your tabs of the application, most recently active first, and which one the surface tools act on.         |
| `relay_select-tab`    | Choose another of your tabs. Revisions differ between tabs, so observe again after choosing.               |
| `relay_pair`          | Development only: pair with the code the tab shows.                                                        |
| `relay_stop`          | End agent access to a tab, as the person's Stop does; a host closes its hidden session.                    |
| `surface_observe`     | The tab's controls under one revision: what can be done now, why not the rest, values, filtered and paged. |
| `surface_set-field`   | Set a field through the page's own setter.                                                                 |
| `surface_run-control` | Run a button or switch through the page's own handler.                                                     |
| `surface_load-more`   | Ask a list to load more.                                                                                   |
| `surface_ledger`      | Every act and refusal on the tab, with who asked and the revisions it spanned.                             |
| `surface_read`        | What the page shows the person (headings, text, fields, tables), redacted and bounded, with a cursor.     |
| `surface_wait`        | Wait until a condition on the page holds (text appears, the page goes quiet), at most two minutes.        |

These are `domainActions`' default set: a fixed tool list whatever the page holds. `surface_read` and `surface_wait` are answered by the tab's auto surface ([Reading the page](auto-surface.md#reading-the-page)); a tab without one answers them with the reason, and `content: false` on `createRelay` leaves them out. Pass `domains` to `createRelay` for the application's own parameterized actions (for example the set `@summationai/axe-surface/auto` builds). The usual `axe_state`, `axe_continue`, and `axe_resume` tools are there too, so a control that declares `requires` or a handoff climbs the ladder exactly as it does on a server.

An act whose click navigates the page (a link, a form that posts and reloads) is answered `ok` with `navigated: true` just before the page unloads: the tab sees the navigation begin (`beforeunload`) and says so before its connection closes. An act the page never answers for any other reason (it crashed or closed, or `actTimeoutMs` passed) is `unavailable` with `details.reason: "outcome_unknown"` and `retryable: false`: the act was sent and may have taken effect, so the agent is told to observe before acting again, nothing retries it automatically, and a retry with the same `idempotencyKey` returns the same answer instead of running it twice ([S-RELAY-14]).

The first surface tool call pins a tab: by default the most recently active one, and it stays the agent's tab until the agent chooses another with `relay_select-tab`. A tab another tab became active in front of does not change under the agent.

## Approvals and Stop

A high-risk control (an effect with `risk: "high"`) or one whose effect declares `confirm` does not run on the agent's first call. In an attended tab the page shows "The agent asks to: Delete the plan" with Approve and Deny, and the agent receives `unavailable` with `details.reason: "approval_required"` and a sentence to say to the person. After the person approves, the agent's next identical call (same entry, text, and `expectedRev`) runs it once. Deny makes that call `forbidden` with `approval_denied`. An approval lapses after five minutes, and a new revision needs a new one. Change the rule with `requireApproval`:

<!-- include: examples/relay/page.ts#approval -->
```ts
// Only high-risk controls wait for the person; a control that declares confirm runs without it.
export const strict = connectRelay(surface, {
  url: "wss://relay.yogastudio.example/tab",
  getToken: () => "token-from-your-backend",
  requireApproval: (row) => row.effect?.risk === "high",
});
```
<!-- /include -->

### Approvals in the agent

A tab that takes approvals from the agent (unattended, or `approvals: "agent"` or `"both"`) does not wait for a panel nobody sees. When it holds an act, the relay asks the person through MCP elicitation on the calling agent's own session, in the same tool call:

| The client declares | The act | What the person sees | Then |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| form elicitation | not sensitive | A confirm in the agent's UI: "Approve “Lock January” on Plan Board? It changes locks, risk high." with the act's exact text | Approve runs the act in the same tool call. Decline or dismiss refuses it (`forbidden`, `approval_denied`). |
| URL elicitation | sensitive, or the client has no form mode | An offer to open the relay's approval page, `/approve/<id>`: single use, short-lived (`linkTtlMs`, five minutes), bound to the approval, the person, and the request | The tool call waits for the decision on the page, then runs or refuses the act. Declining to open the page refuses it. |
| no elicitation | any | Nothing | The agent gets `approval_required` with instructions, and the approval page link (`details.approvalUrl`) when the relay serves one. After the person approves there, the agent's identical call runs once. |

On a decision the relay tells the tab (`approve` or `deny`), the tab grants its gates exactly as the panel's Approve does (the relay gate and an auto-derived surface's own gate), records the decision in its ledger (`op: "approve"` or `"deny"`, actor `<principal> (approved in the agent's MCP client)` or `(approved on the relay's approval page)`), and the relay sends the act again, which the page's own checks decide. The approval stays bound to the entry, op, text, and `expectedRev`, and is used once. A tool call the client cancels while the person decides runs nothing; the decision stays with the tab for the agent's identical retry.

An act is sensitive when it targets a sensitive entry, or when `approvals.sensitive` says so. The approval page needs to know who opened it: `approvals.identify(request)` returns the principal and tenant of the person's own session on the relay's domain, and the page refuses anyone else. Without `identify` (outside development) the relay serves no approval page and never offers URL mode:

<!-- include: examples/relay/server.ts#approvals -->
```ts
// Approvals asked through the agent (unattended tabs). A form in the agent's MCP client needs
// nothing here. The approval page (URL mode, for sensitive acts) needs to know who opened it:
// the person's own session on the relay's domain, never anything the agent sent.
declare function sessionFromCookie(request: Request): { userId: string; studioId: string } | null;

export const unattended = createRelay({
  secret: process.env["RELAY_TOKEN_SECRET"]!,
  origins: ["https://app.yogastudio.example"],
  agentAuth: {
    verifier,
    identify: (authInfo) =>
      typeof authInfo.extra?.["sub"] === "string" && typeof authInfo.extra?.["org"] === "string"
        ? { principal: authInfo.extra["sub"], tenant: authInfo.extra["org"] }
        : null,
  },
  baseUrl: "https://relay.yogastudio.example",
  approvals: {
    identify: (request) => {
      const s = sessionFromCookie(request);
      return s ? { principal: s.userId, tenant: s.studioId } : null;
    },
    // Links work once, for five minutes by default.
    linkTtlMs: 300_000,
    // Decided on the page rather than in a form: anything touching payments.
    sensitive: (row) => row.object === "billing",
  },
});

// A host's own Stop control (its watch page) ends the person's sessions.
export function stopFor(userId: string, studioId: string): number {
  return unattended.stop({ principal: userId, tenant: studioId });
}
```
<!-- /include -->

An elicitation is shown to the person by their MCP client; the model cannot answer it (the MCP specification requires the client to put it before the user). So a form decision is the person's as far as the client is trustworthy. The approval page moves the decision to a page the relay serves, outside the client, which is why sensitive acts go there. The relay never accepts an approval from a tool argument: `confirm: true`, text, or anything else the model sends is not a decision.

An attended page can take approvals from both places, whichever answers first:

<!-- include: examples/relay/page.ts#both -->
```ts
// A person is looking, but may also approve from the agent's client: whichever answers first.
export const either = connectRelay(surface, {
  url: "wss://relay.yogastudio.example/tab",
  getToken: () => "token-from-your-backend",
  approvals: "both",
});
```
<!-- /include -->

### Stop

Stop disconnects the tab, revokes its token at the relay, and refuses every later act on that tab with `forbidden`; the agent is told the person stopped it. Stop lasts for the page: a reload connects again only if your page calls `connectRelay` again. Leaving or reloading the page is not Stop: the relay keeps the tab for a reconnect, and an act sent while it reloads waits for the new page. Framework cleanup calls `connection.disconnect()`, not `connection.stop()`.

To render the indicator with your own design system, turn it off and drive yours from `onStatus`; your UI must then show that an agent is connected and offer Stop, Approve, and Deny:

<!-- include: examples/relay/page.ts#own-indicator -->
```ts
// Render the indicator with your own design system: turn the built-in one off and drive yours
// from onStatus. Your UI must show that an agent is connected and offer Stop and the approvals.
export function connectWithOwnIndicator(
  s: Surface,
  render: (status: RelayStatus, controls: RelayConnection) => void,
): RelayConnection {
  const connection: RelayConnection = connectRelay(s, {
    url: "wss://relay.yogastudio.example/tab",
    getToken: () =>
      fetch("/api/relay-token", { method: "POST" }).then(
        async (r) => ((await r.json()) as { token: string }).token,
      ),
    indicator: false,
    onStatus: (status) => render(status, connection),
  });
  return connection;
}
```
<!-- /include -->


The indicator is kept out of an auto-derived surface: its host carries `data-surface-ignore`, and `@summationai/axe-surface/auto` never reads it. An agent cannot press Approve, Deny, or Stop. If you render your own indicator, mark its root `data-surface-ignore` too.
## Tenant switches and server rendering

When the person changes tenant (or signs in as someone else) without a reload, call `rekey`. The client leaves the relay under the old identity, which drops the tab's record and revokes its token, then connects with a fresh token:

<!-- include: examples/relay/page.ts#rekey -->
```ts
// The person switched studios (tenants) without a reload: leave under the old identity and
// connect again with a token for the new one. No agent of the old tenant reaches the page after.
export function onStudioSwitched(): void {
  relay.rekey();
}
```
<!-- /include -->

Importing `@summationai/axe-relay/client` touches no `window`, `document`, or `WebSocket`, so a page rendered on the server can load it in an effect:

<!-- include: examples/relay/page.ts#dynamic -->
```ts
// With server-side rendering, load the client in an effect: importing it touches no window,
// document, or WebSocket, and connecting happens only in the browser.
export async function startRelayInBrowser(s: Surface): Promise<() => void> {
  const { connectRelay: connect, localMcpService: local } =
    await import("@summationai/axe-relay/client");
  const connection = connect(s, local());
  return () => connection.disconnect();
}
```
<!-- /include -->

Use `disconnect()` for framework and route cleanup. It closes that page connection without
revoking the tab, so a remount can reattach. Reserve `stop()` for an explicit decision by the
person to end agent access.

## Production

The browser side needs only `@summationai/axe-relay` (its `client` entry imports nothing at runtime) alongside `@summationai/axe-surface`. The standalone service under [`mcp/`](../mcp/README.md) owns `@summationai/axe-mcp`, the MCP SDK, `ws`, and the relay server. A web application that only connects its tabs installs none of those server dependencies.

A production relay authenticates both sides: tabs with relay tokens your backend minted, agents with OAuth access tokens.

<!-- include: examples/relay/server.ts#production -->
```ts
const relay = createRelay({
  // The key the backend mints relay tokens with.
  secret: process.env["RELAY_TOKEN_SECRET"]!,
  // The pages that may connect a tab: exact origins, subdomains, or any port on localhost.
  origins: ["https://app.yogastudio.example", "https://*.yogastudio.example"],
  // Agents: an OAuth 2.1 resource server. `identify` says who a verified token speaks for; an
  // agent reaches only the tabs of that principal and tenant.
  agentAuth: {
    verifier,
    requiredScopes: ["relay"],
    resource: "https://relay.yogastudio.example/mcp",
    identify: (authInfo) => {
      const sub = authInfo.extra?.["sub"];
      const org = authInfo.extra?.["org"];
      return typeof sub === "string" && typeof org === "string"
        ? { principal: sub, tenant: org }
        : null;
    },
  },
  onEvent: (event) => console.info("[relay]", JSON.stringify(event)),
});

// Behind a TLS terminator: tabs connect to wss://relay.yogastudio.example/tab and agents to
// https://relay.yogastudio.example/mcp.
await relay.listen({ host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 });
```
<!-- /include -->

- The relay token is a JSON Web Token signed with HMAC-SHA256: `sub` is the principal, `org` the tenant, `aud` is `axe-relay` (the relay's `audience` option), and it lives at most a day. `mintRelayToken` makes one; any JWT library that signs HS256 does too. `verifyRelayToken` checks one. Or pass `authenticateTab` to check tokens your own way.
- `origins` takes exact origins, `https://*.example.com` (subdomains, not the apex), and `http://localhost:*` (any port), or a function. Mirror your application's own rule; a pattern outside these forms is an error when the relay is created.
- `tenants` restricts the relay to some tenants; a tab or an agent of another is refused.
- `attach(server)` serves the relay on a Node HTTP server you already run; `handle(request)` serves `/mcp` from a framework that gives you Web requests (the tab endpoint needs the server's upgrade event).
- The relay holds tabs in memory, in one process. Run one relay process per deployment, or route each person to one (their tabs and their agent must reach the same process).
- `axe relay --stdio --principal <p> --tenant <t> --origin <url>`, with `AXE_RELAY_SECRET` set, runs a relay for one local agent acting as one named principal.

## Connecting agents

- **Codex**, local service: set `AXE_MCP_AGENT_KEY`, then `codex mcp add agent-experience --url http://127.0.0.1:4717/mcp --bearer-token-env-var AXE_MCP_AGENT_KEY`.
- **Claude Code**, local service: connect its HTTP MCP configuration to `http://127.0.0.1:4717/mcp` with `Authorization: Bearer <AXE_MCP_AGENT_KEY>`.
- **Claude Code**, production: `claude mcp add --transport http surface https://relay.yogastudio.example/mcp`; Claude Code finds the authorization server from the protected-resource metadata (see [MCP](mcp.md), "OAuth") and signs the person in.
- **Other MCP clients**: the same URL over Streamable HTTP with a bearer token. The server's instructions tell the agent to call `relay_tabs` first, pair when needed, and use the Surface tools instead of generic browser automation.

## Security model

The relay puts a live, signed-in page within reach of an agent, so it states what it guarantees ([S-RELAY-1] to [S-RELAY-13]) and [Security](security.md) lists the threats:

- The page is authoritative. An act runs through the page's `surface.act` with the page's act queue, revision check, availability, and handler; the relay decides nothing about the application.
- A tab authenticates with a relay token your backend minted for the signed-in person, from an allowed origin. The page's session cookie never goes to the relay.
- An agent reaches only the tabs whose token named its own principal and tenant. Another principal's tab id is as unknown as a made-up one.
- Tokens expire; the page renews in-band, and a connection whose token lapses is closed. Stop revokes the token.
- Every act is in the tab's ledger with the actor `<principal> (agent via relay)`.
- A sensitive field's value never leaves the page: the observation, the ledger, and the frames carry no value for it. The application's `objects` do cross; keep private data out of them.
- High-risk acts wait for the person's approval: in the page when attended, in the agent's MCP client (elicitation) or on the relay's single-use approval page when unattended. No tool argument is ever an approval.
- Revisions are the tab's, offset so that a revision read before a reload, or from another tab, never passes the check.

## Limits

- A tab is one page instance; nothing survives the page but what the application persists. The agent's view is as fresh as its last read: every surface tool call first asks the tab for its current table.
- The relay is in memory and in one process: tab records, pairings, and revocations reset on restart.
- The approval gate is in the page: a script already running in the page can press Approve, as it could click any control.
- In unattended mode the relay is trusted to carry the person's decision to the tab: a tab that takes approvals from the agent accepts `approve` from its relay connection. An attended tab (`approvals: "page"`, the default) accepts none.
- A form approval is only as trustworthy as the MCP client that renders it. A client that times out long tool calls may give up while the person decides; the decision then waits in the tab for the agent's retry.
- Page text (names, reasons, values, the tab's title and path) reaches the agent as data; the MCP instructions tell it never to treat that text as instructions.

## Next steps

- [Surface](surface.md): registering controls the relay then serves.
- [MCP](mcp.md): the derived server, HTTP sessions, and OAuth.
- [Security](security.md): the relay's threats and mitigations.

# docs/host.md

# Unattended mode: the agent uses the app for you

The person signs in once in the agent's own UI. The SDK then runs the application in a private browser for that person, and the agent acts through the application's real controls, availability, reasons, and handlers. There is no pairing code or ordinary application tab to keep open. If the application itself still requires login, the host can briefly present that private session's standard sign-in controls as a secure semantic form; after sign-in it returns to unattended operation. This is the provider's default desktop/mobile adapter; browser-native WebMCP is an additional direct path where supported, and an attended relay remains a diagnostic fallback.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Agent<br/>signed in with OAuth] <-- MCP: HTTP + OAuth, or stdio --> H[Host<br/>createHost / axe host]
  H -- one browser context per person --> B[Headless Chromium:<br/>the app's own page<br/>SurfaceProvider + relay]
  B <-- WebSocket on loopback,<br/>relay token the host minted --> R[Relay, in the host]
  H -. sessionFor: the app's session .-> B
```

`@summationai/axe-host` is the host. For each principal and tenant an agent authenticates as, it starts an isolated Playwright browser context on the agent's first tool call, applies an application session when `sessionFor` returns one, injects the relay connection before any page script runs, opens the application, and waits until the page's surface is connected. Every tool call then routes to that person's private tab. The rules are [S-HOST-1] to [S-HOST-10] in [spec/SURFACE.md](../spec/SURFACE.md) §9.2.

## What the application needs

Initialize the application with `axe surface init`. The default adds the relay browser client and makes the generated provider connect only when a host injects a scoped connection (`window.__AXE_RELAY__`). Pass `--browser-only` only when this application will never support a desktop/mobile provider session:

<!-- include: examples/host/page.ts#page -->
```ts
const handle = autoSurface({ root: document.body });
// In the host's hidden browser, `window.__AXE_RELAY__` is set before this script runs, and
// injectedRelay() returns it (unattended: no indicator, approvals through the agent). In a
// person's own browser it returns null, and nothing connects.
const options = injectedRelay();
if (options) connectRelay(handle.surface, options);
```
<!-- /include -->

It is also always on inside a hosted session, whatever the application's own flag says there: the generated gate is `enabled = <your flag or the development gate> || injectedRelay() !== null`. `injectedRelay()` reads the global when called and is null on the server, so a server render is unaffected.

<!-- include: examples/host/page.ts#gate -->
```ts
// A feature flag that is off for the person must still let a hosted session turn the surface on.
export const surfaceOn = (flag: boolean): boolean => flag || injectedRelay() !== null;
```
<!-- /include -->

An integration written by hand needs the same two things: connect when `injectedRelay()` returns a connection, and do not let a flag that is off for the person keep the provider from mounting in a hosted session. `--start <path>` opens the page the agent starts on (for example `/dashboards`). The attended alternative, where the person's own tab connects to a relay (`axe surface init --relay-dev`, or `--relay <url>`), keeps the injected connection first:

<!-- include: examples/host/page.ts#fallback -->
```ts
// The attended fallback: the person's own tab connects to your relay when no host injected one.
export const relayConnection = (dev: boolean) =>
  injectedRelay() ??
  (dev
    ? {
        url: "wss://relay.yogastudio.example/tab",
        getToken: () =>
          fetch("/api/relay-token", { method: "POST" }).then(
            async (r) => ((await r.json()) as { token: string }).token,
          ),
      }
    : null);
```
<!-- /include -->

## Local development

The host needs a Chromium that Playwright can start. The repository's Playwright browsers work; otherwise install one with `npx playwright install chromium` (or pass `browser.executablePath`).

1. Start your application as usual, for example on `http://localhost:5173`.
2. Sign in once, in a visible browser the host opens for you:

   ```sh
   npx @summationai/axe host login http://localhost:5173
   ```

   Sign in as you normally would, then press Enter in the terminal (or close the window). The signed-in session (cookies and `localStorage`, a Playwright storage state) is saved to `.axe/host-state.json`, readable only by you. It is your session: keep it out of version control (add `.axe/` to `.gitignore`) and log in again when it expires. `--state <file>` saves it elsewhere.

3. Connect the agent. Let Claude Code start the host itself:

   ```sh
   claude mcp add summation -- npx @summationai/axe host --dev --stdio --app http://localhost:5173
   ```

   Or start it in a terminal, which prints the exact commands and configuration for your machine, with absolute paths to Node, the CLI, and the saved session:

   ```sh
   npx @summationai/axe host --dev --app http://localhost:5173 --name summation
   ```

   ```text
   axe host: serving MCP on http://127.0.0.1:4718/mcp for http://localhost:5173 (development, loopback only)
   Signed in with the session saved in /Users/you/app/.axe/host-state.json.

   Connect Claude Code to this host (HTTP):
     claude mcp add --transport http summation http://127.0.0.1:4718/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer axh_…"
   Or let Claude Code start the host itself (stop this one first):
     claude mcp add summation -- /usr/local/bin/node /Users/you/app/node_modules/axe/dist/index.js host --dev --stdio --app http://localhost:5173 --state /Users/you/app/.axe/host-state.json

   Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json), which starts the host itself:
     {
       "mcpServers": {
         "summation": {
           "command": "/usr/local/bin/node",
           "args": ["/Users/you/app/node_modules/axe/dist/index.js", "host", "--dev", "--stdio", "--app", "http://localhost:5173", "--state", "/Users/you/app/.axe/host-state.json"]
         }
       }
     }

   Watch the hidden session: http://127.0.0.1:4718/watch/5f0c…
   ```

   Claude Desktop starts its servers with its own working directory, so use the printed configuration with absolute paths rather than `npx`.

4. Ask the agent to do something in the app ("open the Q3 dashboard and add a filter for EMEA"). Its first tool call starts the hidden session; `relay_tabs` shows it, `surface_read` returns what the page shows, `surface_observe` lists the page's controls, `surface_wait` waits for slow work, and `host_screenshot` shows the page. A consequential act asks you in Claude first. Open the watch URL to follow along; Stop there closes the session.

`--start <path>` opens a page other than the app's root, `--port` changes the HTTP port (default 4718), and `--headed` shows the browser window for debugging.

`axe host login` is a development shortcut: one person's session, captured once, reused for the one development identity (`dev`). Production authentication is OAuth in the agent plus your application's `sessionFor`, below. The command line runs development only.

The same in code:

<!-- include: examples/host/dev.ts#dev -->
```ts
// Loopback only, one identity ("dev"), the session `axe host login` saved, and a key for /mcp.
const host = createHost({
  appUrl: "http://localhost:5173",
  startPath: "/dashboards",
  dev: true,
  sessionFor: storageStateSession(".axe/host-state.json"),
});
const address = await host.listen({ port: 4718 });
console.log(`MCP: ${address.mcpUrl} (Bearer ${host.devAgentKey}); watch: ${address.watchUrl}`);
```
<!-- /include -->

What development mode allows: the host listens on loopback only (`0.0.0.0` is refused) and refuses any request whose peer or `Host` header is not loopback, so a web page cannot reach it through DNS rebinding. `/mcp` needs the printed key, or stdio. The watch page lives behind a random path.

## What the agent sees

| Tool                                                                        | What it does                                                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `relay_tabs`                                                                | The hosted tab of the person the agent signed in as (started on the first call).                         |
| `surface_observe`                                                           | The page's controls under one revision: what can be done now, why not the rest, values.                  |
| `surface_set-field`, `surface_run-control`, `surface_load-more`             | Act through the page's own setters, handlers, and lists.                                                  |
| `surface_ledger`                                                            | Every act and refusal in the tab, with who asked.                                                         |
| `surface_read`                                                              | What the page shows the person (headings, text, fields, tables), redacted and bounded: status, results, reports. |
| `surface_wait`                                                              | Wait until something shows on the page (a status, a finished report), at most two minutes.                 |
| `relay_stop`                                                                | End the session (the agent's next call may start a new one).                                              |
| `host_screenshot`                                                           | A PNG of the page as it is now (MCP image content), to show the person a result.                          |

There is no `relay_pair`: the tab is the agent's by identity. Navigation is through the UI too: links, and the derived `page:navigate` entry for same-origin paths.

A consequential control (high risk, or one the derived surface holds for approval) is asked of the person in the agent's own UI, through MCP elicitation, within the same tool call ([Relay](relay.md), "Approvals"). Nobody sees the hidden page, so nothing is ever approved there; a client that cannot ask the person gets `approval_required` and the act does not run.

## Production

A production host authenticates agents with OAuth access tokens (the SDK is a resource server; your authorization server issues the tokens) and gets each person's application session from your `sessionFor`.

<!-- include: examples/host/production.ts#production -->
```ts
const host = createHost({
  appUrl: "https://app.yogastudio.example",
  startPath: "/schedule",
  sessionFor,
  // Agents: an OAuth 2.1 resource server. `identify` names the person and tenant a verified
  // token speaks for; each gets its own browser context, started on their first tool call.
  agentAuth: {
    verifier,
    requiredScopes: ["app:act"],
    resource: "https://agents.yogastudio.example/mcp",
    identify: (authInfo) => {
      const sub = authInfo.extra?.["sub"];
      const org = authInfo.extra?.["org"];
      return typeof sub === "string" && typeof org === "string"
        ? { principal: sub, tenant: org }
        : null;
    },
  },
  // Where MCP clients find your authorization server (RFC 9728).
  protectedResource: {
    resource: "https://agents.yogastudio.example/mcp",
    authorizationServers: ["https://auth.yogastudio.example"],
    scopesSupported: ["app:act"],
  },
  // The identity provider's pages, if a session ever needs them; every other origin is refused.
  allowedOrigins: ["https://auth.yogastudio.example"],
  maxSessions: 50,
  idleMs: 10 * 60_000,
  onEvent: (event) => console.info("[host]", JSON.stringify(event)),
});

// Behind a TLS terminator at https://agents.yogastudio.example. The relay the hosted pages
// connect to runs inside this process, on loopback.
await host.listen({ host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 });
```
<!-- /include -->

Connect Claude Code with `claude mcp add --transport http summation https://agents.yogastudio.example/mcp`: it reads the protected-resource metadata, finds your authorization server, and signs the person in, in its own UI.

### sessionFor: the application issues the session

The SDK does not issue application sessions and never sees a password. `sessionFor` receives the verified identity (`principal`, `tenant`, and `authInfo`, the verified access token) and returns what the browser context starts with: `cookies`, `headers` (sent to the application's origin only), a `storageState`, or `localStorage` entries. Return null to refuse.

If this is a valid identity that still needs to sign in to the application, throw `SessionLoginRequired` with a trusted, short-lived application URL:

```ts
import { SessionLoginRequired, type SessionFor } from "@summationai/axe-host";

const sessionFor: SessionFor = async ({ principal, tenant }) => {
  const exchange = await appSessions.exchange({ principal, tenant });
  if (exchange.status === "login_required") {
    throw new SessionLoginRequired({
      url: exchange.loginUrl,
      instructions: "Sign in on the application's page, then return to your assistant.",
      whatAgentShouldSayToUser: "Please connect your application account so I can continue.",
      expiresAt: exchange.expiresAt,
    });
  }
  if (exchange.status === "refused") return null;
  return { cookies: exchange.cookies };
};
```

The host returns a native `needs_human` result, never asks the model for credentials, and keeps the original tool request in memory. After the person signs in, `axe_resume` calls `sessionFor` again and replays that request. The resume token is bound to the verified principal and tenant, expires with the login URL, and returns the stored result on duplicate resumes. The login page must bind its opaque request to the same identity and make it single-use; do not put a username, password, or application session in the URL.

<!-- include: examples/host/production.ts#session-for -->
```ts
// The application, not the SDK, issues the session: here a short-lived one minted for the user
// the agent's access token names, set as the app's own session cookie. Return null to refuse.
const sessionFor: SessionFor = async ({ principal, tenant, authInfo }) => {
  if (!authInfo?.scopes.includes("app:act")) return null;
  const session = await mintAgentSession({
    userId: principal,
    orgId: tenant,
    scopes: authInfo.scopes,
  });
  return {
    cookies: [
      {
        name: "app_session_jwt",
        value: session.jwt,
        url: "https://app.yogastudio.example",
        expires: Math.floor(session.expiresAt / 1000),
        httpOnly: true,
        secure: true,
        sameSite: "Lax",
      },
    ],
  };
};
```
<!-- /include -->

Two ways an application implements it:

- **A session from your identity provider.** Your backend asks the provider for a short-lived session for the verified user (most providers can mint or exchange one server-side for a user they know, for example after an OAuth token exchange), and `sessionFor` sets it as the session cookie your app already reads.
- **An agent session you issue.** Your backend signs a short-lived "agent session" for the user and tenant, and your session middleware accepts it like its own, marked as the agent's so your audit log and permissions can tell. This keeps the provider out of the loop and lets you narrow what an agent session may do.

Either way, bind it to the identity the verified token names, keep it short-lived (the host starts a new context, and asks again, after `idleMs`), and scope it to what the agent is allowed to do. `cookieSession(fn)` is a shorthand for a `sessionFor` that returns cookies.

### Generic sign-in fallback: the same hosted browser

An application does not need a session broker to participate. When its live Surface profile reports `authentication.state: "signed-out"`, the host pauses the agent's request and returns an `application_login_required` handoff. The linked page is served by `@summationai/axe-host` and presents the ordinary, visible HTML fields and actions from the exact Playwright page and browser context the agent will use as a clean provider-branded form. It does not imitate the application page or show a screenshot. Each step is bound to the exact current document and form revision; one submit applies all values and the chosen action to that private page, and a page change makes an old step unusable. Polls never overlap, a submission stays visibly in progress while the application advances, and a temporary connection failure preserves the current fields and retries instead of claiming the link expired. This handles standard first-party sign-in forms and common multi-step forms without a remote-control toolbar.

The MCP client presents the handoff through its native URL mode when available, producing a Sign in action instead of exposing the capability URL as chat text. The agent presents it once. While its page is actively polling, another application call receives `application_login_pending` without another URL; if the page was closed and has stopped polling, the same URL can be presented again. Framework-only DOM remounts preserve the person's entered value and do not become a new visible step; the page waits for changed authentication semantics to settle before replacing the form. Password visibility is a local eye control inside the field, never a primary action, and toggling it preserves the value. If the application renders or enables its submit button only after processing the field's input event, the host re-reads the same semantic form after filling and uses that newly available primary action; otherwise it submits the exact bound form. All detection is based on standard HTML and accessibility semantics, with no connector-specific selectors or labels.

As soon as a fresh Surface observation reports `signed-in`, the form is replaced by a visually distinct green completion screen. It deliberately remains on screen instead of attempting `window.close()`, which embedded agent browsers handle inconsistently; the person can close it explicitly and return to the assistant. Progress text distinguishes initial submission, waiting for the named application, and an unusually slow sign-in. If the person returns to the agent immediately after submitting, `axe_resume` waits briefly for the application's Surface to report `signed-in` instead of returning a premature loading conflict. It then replays the original request once but keeps the page's status endpoint alive long enough to show completion. A genuinely expired or ended session instead gets an amber terminal page with instructions to start again.

This entire fallback is provider infrastructure. The consuming application adds no login endpoint, callback, iframe, session broker, Playwright dependency, or MCP code. Its only contract is an accurate live profile:

```ts
profile: () => ({
  id: "example-app",
  name: "Example App",
  authentication: { state: auth.loading ? "unknown" : auth.user ? "signed-in" : "signed-out" },
});
```

The handoff URL is an expiring capability bound in memory to the verified principal, tenant, hosted tab, and original request. The page accepts a bounded semantic form submission only from its own origin. Field values are sent directly to the bound browser page and are never returned by MCP, Surface, screenshots, ledgers, or events; the handoff never exposes cookies, storage, or relay tokens. Production requires HTTPS. The generic form deliberately does not collect credentials after a redirect to a different identity-provider origin: Google, Microsoft, enterprise SSO, passkeys, and similar federated methods need a provider OAuth connector or `sessionFor`, so credentials stay on the identity provider's own page.

`sessionFor` is still preferable when the provider and application can exchange identity silently: it avoids showing a browser and starts already signed in. The session-bound view is the generic fallback that preserves a zero-backend application installation.

### Deployment

- The host runs one Chromium and one browser context per active person, in one process, with its relay inside on loopback. Each context holds a full page of your application: measure one, size `maxSessions` from it, and route each person to one host process.
- Install a browser where the host runs (`npx playwright install chromium --with-deps` in the image), or pass `browser.executablePath`, or `browser.launch` for a remote browser. `playwright-core` is a dependency of `@summationai/axe-host` only; the application's pages never load it.
- With a relay you run yourself, pass it as `relay` with `relayUrl` and `relaySecret`, and forward its events to `relayEvent` so Stop there closes the hosted session. `extraTools` (in `@summationai/axe-mcp`) and `handleAgent` with `relayAgentContext` (in `@summationai/axe-relay/server`) are the pieces the host builds its MCP server from.

## Security model

A server-side browser acting as a person is powerful, so the host states what it guarantees ([S-HOST-1] to [S-HOST-10]) and [Security](security.md) lists the threats:

- **Identity binding.** A session is for exactly the principal and tenant the agent's verified token names. The host mints the page's relay token for that identity only, and the relay serves an agent only its own person's tab ([S-RELAY-3]). A tenant change is another session.
- **Isolation.** One browser context per identity: no cookie, storage, cache, or permission is shared between two people. They share only the browser process.
- **No pairing, safely.** Pairing exists to prove that the person at the tab is the person the agent speaks for. Here the host opens the tab itself, for the identity the agent signed in as, so there is nothing to prove. The connection is injected only into frames of the application's origin, and the renewal function mints only for those frames.
- **Credentials stay out of the agent.** What `sessionFor` returns is never logged, put in an event, or returned by a tool; headers go only to the application's origin; relay tokens live ten minutes (`tokenTtlSeconds`) and renew in-band. An ordinary `sessionFor` error is not passed on to the agent. `SessionLoginRequired` exposes only the application-supplied login URL and safe instructions. In the generic fallback, one same-origin, revision-bound form submission writes directly to the bound browser page and is never put in MCP content, Surface observations, screenshots, or ledgers.
- **Everything through the UI.** The agent changes nothing except through the page's own controls; the host adds no write tool. `host_screenshot` only reads.
- **Approvals through the agent.** Consequential acts wait for the person in the agent's UI.
- **Navigation stays on the application** (the request-forgery defense). A navigation to any origin other than the application's and `allowedOrigins` is refused and the page stays where it was; `restrict: "all"` refuses every other request too. Cloud metadata addresses are never reachable, and service workers, which could fetch around these rules, are blocked. Each refusal is an event naming the origin.
- **Bounded.** `maxSessions` and `idleMs` bound the browsers a host runs; Stop by the person or the owner holds an identity until it is resumed; revoking the agent's OAuth grant ends its access.

Threats that remain yours: the blast radius of an agent session (narrow what your agent session may do, and audit it; every act is in the tab's ledger under `<principal> (agent via relay)`, and `onEvent` records sessions and refusals); subresource requests to other origins, which `restrict: "navigations"` allows (use `restrict: "all"` for an application that loads nothing from elsewhere, and an egress policy for the host); and page text, which reaches the agent as data and must never be treated as instructions.

## Limits

- Everything is in memory in one process: sessions, the relay's tabs, and Stop holds reset on restart.
- The secure human form handles standard first-party HTML forms, including multi-step username, password, and one-time-code flows. Federated identity-provider redirects, file selection, passkeys, hardware keys, camera/microphone challenges, and CAPTCHAs require a provider OAuth connector, a brokered application session, or another application-supported authentication method.
- Watching is screenshots, polled once a second, in development; there is no live stream.
- An act whose click navigates the page (a link, a form that posts and reloads) is answered `ok` with `navigated: true` just before the page unloads, and the agent is told to observe the new page. An act whose page goes away without a navigation it could see (a crash, a closed page), or does not answer in time, is `unavailable` with `details.reason: "outcome_unknown"` and `retryable: false`: it was sent and may have taken effect, so it is neither retried nor reported as nothing applied ([S-RELAY-14]).
- The development storage state is one person's cookies. It expires like any session, and anyone who can read the file can use it.

## Next steps

- [Relay](relay.md): the relay the host connects its pages to, approvals in the agent's UI, and the attended fallback.
- [Easy mode](auto-surface.md): what the surface derives from the page, and how to refine it.
- [MCP](mcp.md): sessions, OAuth, and elicitation.
- [Security](security.md): the threat model.

# docs/chatgpt-plugin.md

# ChatGPT consumer path

The seamless path for a nontechnical person is an ordinary public ChatGPT plugin backed by the provider-operated Agent Experience service. “No MCP setup” and “no visible browser automation” are achievable for the user; “no MCP transport” is not, because ChatGPT needs a registered, authenticated way to call code outside the conversation.

The product should never ask the user to understand that distinction. Its language is: **Install Agent Experience**, then, only when their request needs it, **Connect to Acme Analytics** (using the application's actual name).

## What happens

1. The application developer installs `@summationai/axe-surface` and the browser-only part of `@summationai/axe-relay`, mounts `SurfaceProvider`, and enables the injected-host path. Their application does not run or deploy MCP.
2. The provider deploys [`mcp/`](../mcp/README.md) at one stable public HTTPS `/mcp` URL and publishes [`plugins/agent-experience`](../plugins/agent-experience/README.md) against it.
3. The person installs the plugin from ChatGPT's directory. MCP initialization is anonymous and silent; opening ChatGPT does not start OAuth or open a browser.
4. After the person asks to use an application, the plugin searches the trusted connector registry, selects the match, and calls `relay_tabs`. The provider authenticates the agent identity and starts or resumes an isolated hidden session for that connector.
5. The provider uses a short-lived application session when a connector has one. Otherwise it starts the application signed out; the Surface reports that state and the provider offers a secure, session-bound view of the exact private browser for the person to complete the application's existing login. No application backend change is required.
6. The host injects an identity-bound relay before application code runs. The root-mounted Surface stays connected on login, organization selection, tenant selection, and authenticated routes. The visible session page closes after the exceptional human step; ordinary agent work remains inside ChatGPT.
7. The model calls `surface_read` and `surface_observe`, advances any chooser, and completes the task with Surface tools. Consequential controls use ChatGPT's approval flow.

```text
ChatGPT on phone
  └─ installed Agent Experience plugin (silent until a relevant request)
       └─ provider HTTPS /mcp
            ├─ provider identity + application-session exchange
            └─ isolated hidden application browser
                 └─ installed package + page-held Surface
```

The page remains authoritative for its live profile, authentication and context state, controls, revisions, handlers, and ledger. The provider registry owns trusted discovery and bootstrap facts: application URL, allowed origins, identity mapping, and session strategy. The generic MCP runtime owns transport, agent identity, routing, and hidden-browser lifetime; it contains no application workflows or selectors. The application keeps its existing login and user authorization unchanged.

> The provider registry says where an application is and how it may be connected securely. The application's Surface says what the application currently is and what the agent can do there. The MCP contains no application-specific behavior.

## The application contract

The developer installs the browser packages, mounts the generated Surface provider above authentication and context resolution, and connects its profile to the application's existing auth state. That remains the complete application integration boundary: there is no application MCP server, customer-operated relay, auth callback, session broker, or remote-browser service. A connector may add a provider-owned session broker later to make sign-in silent, but it is an optimization rather than a prerequisite.

The injected relay token is a capability from the provider host, not an application credential. It is bound to the authenticated agent identity and tenant, expires quickly, and reaches only the Surface in that isolated browser. It grants no direct application API access.

Credentials are entered only on the application's page inside the provider's secure session view, or through a provider-owned account connection. They are never requested in model-visible chat or set through an agent Surface action.

## What the user must still approve

The website cannot silently enroll itself in a person's ChatGPT account. Plugin installation and OAuth consent are platform trust decisions, just like installing an app and signing in. After public distribution, those are taps in normal ChatGPT UI—not developer mode, a URL, a secret, or a server configuration.

Use a clear “Use in ChatGPT” entry point from the product after publication, but do not imply that opening the website alone grants ChatGPT access. Enterprise administrators may also control plugin availability.

## Fallbacks

- Development pairing remains a diagnostic-only local loop. `local-unattended` validates the hidden-browser interaction shape without claiming a production identity boundary.
- Browser-native WebMCP can remove the remote transport when the agent actually runs in a compatible browser host. It does not currently provide a general ChatGPT iOS path to another app's authenticated session.
- The secure session-bound browser handoff is available when no provider-owned application session exists. It is visible only for the human-only authentication step; the agent's actual task remains unattended. The older attended relay remains diagnostic-only.

## Operational boundary

Hosted browser sessions and relay records are currently process memory. Keep the service behind TLS, apply origin checks and rate limits, and use sticky routing or shared state before running multiple instances. Revoking the OAuth grant ends new agent access; the person can stop a hosted session through the agent approval/UI boundary.

# docs/webmcp.md

# WebMCP

WebMCP is a browser API through which a page registers tools for an agent built into the browser. `@summationai/axe-surface/webmcp` offers a [Surface](surface.md) through it: the page's controls become tools the browser's agent can call, each one running through the page's own surface with its revision guard, availability, and ledger. This page covers the status of the API, what the adapter registers, what it never registers, and what to use where the browser has no WebMCP.

For React easy mode, `<SurfaceProvider webMcp>` enables this direct route. It needs only `@summationai/axe-surface`; no MCP server or relay participates in that route. The recommended desktop-agent integration also installs `@summationai/axe-relay` and connects the same page-held Surface to the separately operated [Agent Experience MCP service](../mcp/README.md), because a generic desktop or headless-browser session does not receive a page's WebMCP tools automatically.

## Status

WebMCP is a draft, and most browsers do not have it. What this page and the adapter rest on, as read on 2026-09-24:

- The specification is a Draft Community Group Report of the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group, dated 17 September 2026 ([webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp](https://webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp/); explainer at [github.com/webmachinelearning/webmcp](https://github.com/webmachinelearning/webmcp)). It exposes `document.modelContext` with `registerTool(tool, { signal })`; aborting the signal unregisters the tool.
- Chrome offers it for local testing behind `chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing` and to sites in an origin trial from Chrome 149 ([developer.chrome.com/docs/ai/webmcp](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/ai/webmcp), updated 7 August 2026; the imperative API page, updated 21 September 2026). Chrome describes the API as under active discussion and subject to change.
- Earlier drafts put the API on the navigator object and had separate methods to provide a whole tool set and to unregister a tool by name. The current draft has neither, and the adapter does not look for them.

Treat the adapter as experimental for as long as the API is. It reaches the browser API in one function each for finding it and registering a tool, so a change in the draft is a small change in the adapter.

## Offering a surface

<!-- include: examples/webmcp/page.ts#expose -->
```ts
import { exposeWebMcp } from "@summationai/axe-surface/webmcp";
import { surface } from "../surface/board";

// Browser-driving agents keep reading window.__surface, whatever the browser supports.
surface.expose(typeof window !== "undefined" ? window : null);

// Registers surface_observe, page read/wait tools when this is an auto surface, and one tool per
// control when document.modelContext exists; otherwise registers nothing and says why. The human
// UI is the same either way.
const webmcp = exposeWebMcp(surface, { actor: "browser-agent" });
if (!webmcp.supported) console.info(`WebMCP not offered: ${webmcp.reason}`);
else void webmcp.ready().then(() => console.info("WebMCP:", webmcp.diagnostic()));

// A single-page app that tears the board down (a route change) closes it too.
export function leaveBoard(): void {
  webmcp.close();
}
```
<!-- /include -->

`exposeWebMcp(surface, options)` returns a handle: `supported` and, when false, `reason`; `tools()`, the names registered now; `ready()`, which resolves when the current registration round has settled; `diagnostic()`, which distinguishes unavailable, registering, ready, degraded, registration error, and closed states; and `close()`, which unregisters everything and stops following the surface. When React's `SurfaceProvider` also has `expose`, the same diagnostic is available at `window.__surface.webMcp()`.

Options:

- `modelContext`: the object to register with. Default: `document.modelContext` when it has `registerTool`. `null` turns the adapter off; an object of your own is for tests and polyfills.
- `prefix`: prepended to every tool name. Default `surface_`.
- `actor`: the `actor` the ledger records for acts made through these tools. Default `webmcp`.
- `unavailable`: `describe` (the default) registers an unavailable control with its reason; `omit` leaves it out until it is available.
- `observe`: register the observe tool. Default true.
- `content`: register read and wait tools when the surface came from `autoSurface`. Default true.
- `run`: wraps each handler run, as `surface.act`'s option does.
- `requestApproval`: trusted application UI for high-risk, confirmation, and `approval_required` controls. It receives the exact observed entry, act, and input and returns a boolean or `{ approved, actor }`. Without it, those calls are refused. It must resolve only from the person's interaction and must never be reachable by the agent.
- `onError`: called when the browser refuses a registration (another script holds the name, a permissions policy forbids tools).

<!-- include: examples/webmcp/page.ts#options -->
```ts
// Leave unavailable controls out instead of describing them, and use a prefix per page so two
// surfaces on one page do not collide.
export const quiet = exposeWebMcp(surface, { unavailable: "omit", prefix: "draft_" });
```
<!-- /include -->

## What is registered

- **`surface_observe`.** Read-only. Returns the observation: every entry's id, name, availability with its reason, and effect, under one revision, as text and as structured content. Sensitive field values are not in it ([S-PRV-1](../spec/SURFACE.md#61-authorization-and-privacy)).
- **`surface_read`.** Read-only, on an auto surface. Returns the headings, text, fields, tables, lists, notices, and named opaque regions that the page shows the person. It is bounded and paginated; private values are withheld and chart values are never guessed.
- **`surface_wait`.** Read-only, on an auto surface. Waits within a bound for visible text, a control's availability, a moved revision, a matching route, or an idle page, and reports what changed and which notices appeared. It is the direct way to follow work such as a report moving from “Preparing” to ready.
- **One tool per control that can be acted on.** An action (a click), a field that is not sensitive (typing text), a collection that can load more. The tool's description is the entry's `describeEntry` line, what the tool does, and for an unavailable control what would unblock it or what a person must do. The input schema takes an optional `expectedRev`, `text` for a field (with the field's own schema and `maxLength`), and `confirm` for a control that asks for confirmation. A control that is not reversible carries the `consequentialHint` annotation, which the draft defines for tools whose effect cannot be undone.

Tool names are the prefix and the entry id, with every character other than letters, digits, `_`, and `-` replaced by `_`: `pick:me:gibbs` becomes `surface_pick_me_gibbs`. Two ids that would share a name, or an id that would take the observe, read, or wait tool's name, get an eight-character hash of the id appended. A name is the same for an id every time, so an agent that learned it keeps it.

## Host compatibility and preflight

The browser is the WebMCP host. A package in the page can register tools only when that browser provides `document.modelContext.registerTool`; it cannot make a generic browser-automation or headless-computer-use session forward those tools to its model. Such a session may still click the ordinary UI, but that is not a Surface tool call and does not gain Surface's revision guard or ledger.

For ChatGPT desktop, use its built-in browser with site tools enabled and a model that supports site tools. OpenAI's [site-tools documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/webmcp) describes that path; an external browser tab, a generic headless browser task, and a nested CLI agent are separate hosts and must not be assumed to inherit the page's tools.

Before asking an agent to act, verify all three layers:

1. `typeof document.modelContext?.registerTool === "function"` — the browser implements imperative WebMCP.
2. `await window.__surface?.webMcp?.()` in a development integration — registration settled with `state: "ready"` (or inspect its per-tool errors when `degraded` or `error`).
3. The browser's Site tools UI lists `surface_observe`, and, for an auto surface, `surface_read` and `surface_wait` — the host actually delivered them to the agent.

If step 1 fails, choose a compatible browser host. If step 2 fails, fix the reported registration errors. If step 3 fails while step 2 says ready, the browser host did not make the registered tools available to that task; changing tool descriptions or prompting the model cannot repair that transport boundary.

Use a fresh agent conversation for a clean acceptance test after installing or updating the page integration. A previous conversation may retain its earlier diagnosis and fallback plan. Also inspect project-local agent configuration: a leftover MCP server for the same application is a separate transport and can cause a nested CLI agent to choose that server even when browser-native Surface is installed.

## What is never registered

- **A sensitive field.** The person types it; no tool can fill it, and no tool text or result carries its value.
- **The ledger.** Acted-on text may be in it under the `keep` policy. `expose` still publishes it for browser-driving agents in the page.
- **A collection with nothing to load.**
- **Anything outside the page.** WebMCP tools run in the page with the user's own session, like `expose`. They add no reader the page did not have and are not a way to reach the surface from a server.

## Acting

A tool call is `surface.act` with the entry's id and op. With `expectedRev`, a page that changed since the agent observed it refuses the act as `conflict` and nothing runs. Without it, the act uses the page's revision at the moment of the call: the agent acts on the page as it is, and the surface's availability and confirmation checks still apply. The tool returns the act's envelope as structured content, one line of text (`Done: Lock March. The page is now at rev 3.`, or why not and what to do), and `isError` when the act was refused.

Every change the surface reports through `subscribe` re-derives the tools. A tool is registered again only when its name, description, schema, or annotations changed, so a revision bump alone costs nothing, and a control that became unavailable is re-registered with its reason (or dropped, with `unavailable: "omit"`).

### Trusted approval

`consequentialHint` is metadata, not an enforcement boundary. The adapter therefore refuses a high-risk action, an action with `confirm`, or an `approval_required` control unless `requestApproval` is configured. When the callback approves an auto-derived gate, the adapter opens that one gate and immediately makes the exact revision-bound act. It records the person's decision before the act in the page's ledger.

```ts
const webmcp = exposeWebMcp(surface, {
  requestApproval: async ({ entry, act }) => {
    // `showApprovalDialog` must resolve only from the person's click.
    const approved = await showApprovalDialog({
      title: entry.name,
      risk: entry.effect?.risk,
      expectedRev: act.expectedRev,
    });
    return { approved, actor: currentMemberName };
  },
});
```

Do not implement this callback with a DOM control included in the surface, a WebMCP tool, a message supplied by the agent, or an automatically accepted browser event.

## Where there is no WebMCP

Nothing is registered, `supported` is false, and the page works as before. The other ways in stay available:

- **Browser-driving agents** read and operate the ordinary page, or use `window.__surface` when their browser channel has JavaScript/CDP access and the application called `surface.expose(window)` ([S-DOM-2](../spec/SURFACE.md#7-browser-agents)). Generic browser clicks are not Surface calls.
- **Server-side agents** reach the same controls through the AXE bridge (`surfaceActions` from `@summationai/axe-surface/axe`, see [Surface](surface.md)) and, for MCP hosts, `@summationai/axe-mcp` ([MCP](mcp.md)), with the authorization rules those need.

An application that exposes its browser surface from one module with `expose(window)`, as the reference application under `examples/` is built to, adds the WebMCP adapter on the next line, as in the example above.

## Headless bridge (experimental)

WebMCP tools exist only in a loaded page, for the agent built into that browser: the explainer lists "fully autonomous workflows" without a browser UI as a non-goal. A desktop agent such as Claude Desktop has no browser of its own, so it cannot reach them directly. `axe host --dev --webmcp --stdio` gives it one: it opens the application in headless Chromium with WebMCP enabled, follows the page's tools through the DevTools protocol's WebMCP domain (the events for tools added and removed, and the command that invokes one), and serves them over MCP on stdio.

```sh
axe host login http://localhost:3000
claude mcp add plan -- npx @summationai/axe host --dev --webmcp --stdio --app http://localhost:3000 --start /plan
```

The page needs no relay connection and no host-specific code: `<SurfaceProvider webMcp>`, `exposeWebMcp`, or any `document.modelContext.registerTool` is the whole integration, and the same registration serves Chrome's built-in agent and ChatGPT's in-app browser. A high-risk control still needs the person: the bridge asks them in the agent's MCP client when it can show a form (elicitation), and otherwise opens a single-use approval page in the person's browser and tells the agent to call again after they decide; see [Approval in a headless page](#approval-in-a-headless-page). The bridge refuses navigations off the application's origin, reports a call whose page navigated or reloaded underneath it as outcome unknown, sends `tools/list_changed` as the page's tools change, and returns each answer only once the tools the call changed are registered again. It needs Chromium 150 or newer (the one Playwright installs qualifies).

Tried on 2026-09-29 against the reference application (`examples/plan-review`, which offers its page surface through `exposeWebMcp` in `app/SurfaceHost.tsx`), headless, signed in as bob at Acme, from a scripted MCP client over stdio:

| Step | Bridge | Relay path (review of 2026-09-25) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start: first `tools/list`, including the browser | 350 ms warm, 1.8 s cold | `relay_tabs` 296 ms, once listening |
| Observe | 2 to 3 ms | 3 to 12 ms |
| Type a forecast | 73 ms, including the wait for the tool list to settle | `surface_set-field` 69 ms |
| Save | 22 ms, and the server's plan shows the value | `surface_run-control` 67 ms |

### Approval in a headless page

A headless page has no one to see the application's `requestApproval` UI. The bridge therefore installs a host approver before any page script runs (`INJECTED_APPROVER_GLOBAL`, a function page code cannot replace), and `exposeWebMcp` asks it instead of the page's UI ([S-WEB-6](../spec/SURFACE.md#8-webmcp-the-browsers-own-agent)). The bridge asks the person:

1. In the agent's own MCP client, when the client declares form elicitation: "Approve “Delete everything” on the board? It changes state, risk high." The answer is recorded in the page's ledger with who gave it, and the act runs or not within the same tool call.
2. Otherwise on a single-use approval page on loopback, opened in the person's browser (and written to the bridge's log). The tool call returns `approval_pending` and nothing runs; after the person decides, the agent's next call of the same tool uses that decision, once, for that control at that revision.

The approval link never appears in anything the agent receives. It is a credential for one decision, and an agent that can reach loopback could otherwise open it and press Approve itself. Tool calls on the page run one at a time, so a question always belongs to exactly one call, and the time the person takes does not count against the call's timeout.

What the bridge does not do yet, in the order it matters:

- **Tool count.** The adapter registers one tool per control: 27 on the reference plan page, and a grid of 50 rows by 12 months would be over 600. The relay path serves a fixed set (`surface_set-field`, `surface_run-control` with an entry id). A compact mode in the adapter, with generic tools taking an entry id, would keep the tool list small for pages with many controls.
- **Annotations.** The DevTools domain carries only a tool's read-only, untrusted-content, and autosubmit hints. A page's `consequentialHint` and `title` do not reach the bridge, so risk reaches the agent only through the tool's description.
- **Identities and production.** The bridge runs one page for one development identity. The per-identity sessions, `sessionFor`, request rules, human sign-in handoff, and OAuth of `createHost` ([Host](host.md)) would move over by making the bridge an alternative to the relay inside `createHost`.
- **Stability.** WebMCP is behind `--enable-features=WebMCP` and its DevTools domain is experimental; both can change with Chromium.

## Bundle

`@summationai/axe-surface/webmcp` remains a separate entry for framework-free use. `SurfaceProvider` imports the small adapter so its `webMcp` prop works without another application dependency; ordinary hooks from `@summationai/axe-surface/react` still tree-shake it when the provider is not used.

## Next steps

- [Surface](surface.md): registering controls, availability, and the revision.
